pages.title: Chips & references
pages.blurb: The chips in text fields, their three states, @{uuid#name:filter} refs, and the filter grammar.

sections.title: Variables and chips
sections.text:
Text fields that understand pipeline syntax colour what they recognise. Two kinds of token matter here:
- Variables ($mood, $outfit.SHOES) read a variable from the Context. They are ordinary text in their own colour, wherever variables can be read: combine and derivation text and the Prompt Assembler template. You edit them like any other word. Each name keeps the same colour everywhere, so $mood in a combine matches the one in the Assembler's variable strip. Hover one to see which module writes it, or that it binds at runtime.
- Ref chips (@{abcd1234#Mood}) embed a fresh pick from another module. They appear where references work: wildcard options and derivation actions. A chip shows the target's name, not its id, and it is one unit: the caret steps over it in one move and Backspace deletes it whole, so you can't half-delete a reference and leave broken syntax behind.
Under the chip the field still stores plain text. Copying a chip copies its syntax, and pasting that syntax anywhere turns back into the same chip.

sections.title: The three states
sections.text:
Resolved
The chip points at something real. A ref chip is tinted with the colour of the module it points at (violet ✦ for a wildcard) and hovering it shows the target's id and option count.
Filtered
A resolved ref chip that narrows its pool. A funnel icon means it carries a sub-category filter, a ban icon means it excludes the null option. Hover shows the filter as it reads and how many options still match, e.g. "3 of 8 options match". Click the chip to edit the filter.
Broken
A red chip with a ? icon: the reference points at a module id that isn't in your library (a placeholder, a deleted module, or one never imported here). Hover shows the name it carries, when the reference stored one. Click it to point it at another module. The editors also outline the field and mark its row (an option, a derivation branch) in red, so you can find it in a long table. At run time it produces nothing and the run reports an "Unresolved reference" warning.
A variable never turns red in the library just because nothing produces it yet: variables can be set at run time (by an injector, a loop, or a Context further up the chain). Its hover says binds at runtime. On the canvas, where the graph is known, a name nothing upstream writes is red with a wavy underline and its hover says no upstream producer. An accessor like $outfit.SHOES whose axis the wildcard doesn't declare is underlined too, because it would render empty.

sections.title: Inserting variables and chips (and placeholders)
sections.text:
Type $ to open the variable list, or @ to open the module list. Keep typing to narrow the list, then pick with Enter or a click.
Picking a wildcard that has sub-categories (or a null option) opens a second step, the filter picker, where you can type a filter expression and tick Exclude null. Press Enter to insert the chip, or leave the expression empty for an unfiltered reference. You can reopen the same picker later by clicking the chip.
Placeholders. To use a variable nothing produces yet, type $ and the name, e.g. $lighting, then a space or a comma (or press Enter when the list is empty). The name is filled in by whatever module later writes $lighting. Until then it renders empty and the Assembler marks it as missing, which is a handy to-do marker while you build a template ahead of its modules.
Module placeholders. The same works for a module you haven't built yet. Type @ and the name, e.g. @castle. When no module has that name, the last row of the list is Placeholder @castle. Pick it to insert a red broken chip under that name. The row it sits in is marked red too, and the list view shows its warning triangle, so it can't be forgotten. Once the module exists, click the chip and point it at the module.

sections.title: @{uuid#name:filter} versus plain @name
sections.text:
A reference is always written with braces and the target's 8-character id. Typing @name does not make a reference: it stays literal text and goes into the prompt as written. Use the @ list to insert the chip and the editor writes the full form for you. The long form has four segments, and only the id is required:
Segment | Example | What it does
id | @{abcd1234} | The module's 8 lowercase hex characters. This is what the engine resolves, so renaming the target never breaks the reference.
#name | @{abcd1234#Mood} | A remembered label. Only used for display, and to tell you what a broken chip used to point at.
:filter | @{abcd1234#Mood:warm or calm} | Only options whose sub-categories satisfy the expression can be picked. Grammar below.
!null | @{abcd1234#Mood:warm!null} | Drops the wildcard's null option from the pool. Without it, the null option always stays in, whatever the filter says.
Where a plain name is enough, reach for a variable instead: $mood reads the value an upstream wildcard already picked, while @{…} rolls the referenced wildcard again, on the spot, from its (optionally filtered) pool.

sections.title: Filter expression grammar
sections.text:
A filter is plain boolean English over the referenced wildcard's sub-category names. Each option is tested against its own tags, and it stays in the pool when the expression is true.
Write | Keeps options that
warm | carry the warm tag
not warm | don't carry warm (options with no tags at all count)
warm and bright | carry both
warm or cool · warm, cool | carry either (a comma is short for or)
not warm and (low or high) | don't carry warm, and carry low or high
not (warm or cool) | carry neither
- Precedence: not binds tightest, then and, then or. So a or b and c means a or (b and c). Use parentheses whenever you mean something else; they nest to any depth.
- Operators are lowercase words. Symbols like !, & or | are not operators, and ! is reserved for the !null flag. Write not warm, never !warm.
- Tag names match exactly, including case. A name can't contain spaces or any of ( ) ! , # : { } @ $, and and, or, not and null are reserved.
- Null is a flag, not a term. To keep the null option out, tick Exclude null (the !null segment); writing not null in the expression is an error.
The filter picker checks the expression as you type. It shows how the expression reads as (fully parenthesised where it matters), how many options match, and flags an unknown sub-category with a did you mean fix. If a valid filter matches no option, the reference resolves to empty at run time and raises a Sub-category filter matched nothing warning that lists the tags the pool actually has (see Warning & conflict types).

sections.title: The flow
sections.text: Figure: Each Context inherits the upstream map; the last write for any $var wins. Steps: WP Context A (rolls $vars) → feeds → WP Context B (adds / overrides) → merged $vars → Prompt Assembler (fills template). Flow diagram of three nodes left to right: WP Context A (rolls $vars), an arrow labelled feeds, WP Context B (adds / overrides), an arrow labelled merged $vars, and Prompt Assembler (fills template). Caption: each Context inherits the upstream map, and the last write for any $var wins.

sections.title: How chaining works
sections.text:
A WP Context node has an optional upstream input. When you connect one Context into another, the downstream Context starts with all the variables the upstream already produced, then runs its own modules on top. Any variable the downstream modules set replaces the upstream value for that name. Variables that the downstream does not touch pass through unchanged.
This makes it easy to build a base Context (character, setting) and then add a second Context that overrides only $style, leaving everything else alone. You can chain as many Contexts as you like — the last value written for any variable is what the Assembler receives.
Use WP Context Injector for one-off variable overrides without adding a full new Context node — it lets you route any node output into a named $variable slot.
Figure: Two WP Context nodes chained into a Prompt Assembler. The upstream Context publishes Starter subject + Starter style. The downstream Context holds a single Override Style row (OVERRIDE badge) that writes $style again. Last write wins, so the assembler reads the override $style while $subject flows through unchanged, resolving 'A picture of a cat, in the style of minimalist line art'. Screenshot of two chained WP Context nodes feeding a WP Prompt Assembler. The upstream WP Context (modules 2 / 2) holds Starter subject and Starter style, which publishes $style. Its context output goes into the upstream input of the second WP Context (modules 1 / 1), which holds a single wildcard row Override Style marked with an OVERRIDE badge, reading '$style · 2 options'. The assembler's template is 'A picture of a $subject, in the style of $style' with $subject and $style as 2 upstream chips, and the preview resolves to 'A picture of a cat, in the style of minimalist line art'. The point: $subject flows through untouched while the later Context's $style wins (last write wins).

sections.title: Internal variables survive the chain
sections.text: When you mark a variable as internal in a module's settings, it travels through the chain to downstream Contexts and combine/derivation modules — it is only hidden at the very end, when the Assembler renders the final prompt string. This means a variable you need for intermediate calculations can be internal from the start, passing through as many chained Contexts as you like, and it still will not appear in the rendered prompt.

sections.title: Constraint modules cross chain boundaries
sections.text:
A constraint module placed in one Context can still apply to a wildcard in a later Context downstream. You can even create a dedicated "constraints" Context that does nothing but hold constraint modules, and chain it before the Context with the target wildcards — the constraints fire when those wildcards roll, exactly as if they were in the same Context.
Separating constraints into their own Context keeps your module stacks readable when you have complex pairing rules across many wildcards.

pages.title: Seeds & loops
pages.blurb: Chain seed, locked seeds, WP Context Loop, iteration vars.

sections.title: The seed and per-module randomness
sections.text:
Every WP Context node has a seed input. At generation time, each module in the stack gets its own independent random stream derived from that seed — so changing the seed changes every module's picks together, but reordering modules does not disturb each other's results.
Inside a module every pick rolls on its own stream too: each fixed value, each derivation rule, and each {a|b} or @{…} in a piece of text. Adding a value, firing another rule or giving another pick more options never changes a roll you already like, and two copies of one module roll independently.
The seed advances automatically after each generation, so you get a fresh set of picks every time you press Generate without editing anything manually.

sections.title: Locked seeds
sections.text:
Any module can have its seed locked. When a module's seed is locked, it always makes the same pick regardless of what the Context seed is doing — perfect for holding a background style or an art direction steady while everything else randomises. Locked modules are also unaffected by the WP Context Loop seed strategies, so they do not vary between iterations.
Lock one module and leave the rest free to compare how different random picks combine with a fixed element — useful for testing whether a style works with a variety of subjects.

sections.title: Seed scope: vary vs hold
sections.text:
Inside a loop, each module decides whether it rides the per-iteration seed or the run's base seed. Every wildcard, combine, fixed-values and derivation module has a Hold across run toggle in its Runtime settings:
- Vary (default) — the module re-rolls every iteration, so its pick changes across the batch.
- Hold across run — the module resolves once at the first iteration and reuses that exact value on every iteration of the run, then re-rolls on the next run. It holds the resolved value, not just the seed: a constrained wildcard keeps its option even as the constraint reshapes the pool, and any nested @{} ref is frozen too — an outfit of @{color} jeans that lands on “green jeans” stays “green jeans” all run. A held derivation works a little differently: it freezes each rule branch's random roll, not which branch fires — the conditions still pick the branch from the current inputs, but a chosen branch always resolves to the same value it landed on at the first iteration. No manual seed lock needed. Flip it from the module's Runtime settings, or right-click the row and pick Hold across run for a two-click toggle.
Hold answers “keep the identity or outfit steady across this batch, but let it re-roll next time.” That's different from a locked seed, which freezes the pick for good — same every run, not just within one run.

sections.title: The flow
sections.text: Figure: The loop fans the chain out into N passes — one resolved prompt per iteration. Steps: WP Context Loop (emits N) → iteration 1…n → WP Context (fresh roll each pass) → $vars → Prompt Assembler (N prompts). Flow diagram of three nodes left to right: WP Context Loop (emits N), an arrow labelled iteration 1…N, WP Context (fresh roll each pass), an arrow labelled $vars, and Prompt Assembler (N prompts). Caption: the loop fans the chain out into N passes, giving one resolved prompt per iteration.

sections.title: Sampler seeds inside a loop
sections.text:
The loop emits a list of prompts — one per iteration — and ComfyUI runs the downstream sampler once per prompt. But a standard KSampler takes a single INT seed, not a list, so every iteration would be sampled with that same seed. If two iterations happen to roll the exact same prompt (e.g. your wildcards landed on the same options twice), the sampler produces the same image for both.
The cleanest fix is to also emit a list of seeds. Drop a WP Seed List between the loop and your sampler:
Figure: Wire the loop's loop_config side-output into the Seed List; downstream the prompt list and seed list pair up by index so each iteration gets its own seed. Steps: WP Context Loop (N prompts) → loop_config → WP Seed List (N seeds) → paired by index → KSampler (N unique images). Flow diagram of three nodes left to right: WP Context Loop (N prompts), an arrow labelled loop_config, WP Seed List (N seeds), an arrow labelled paired by index, and KSampler (N unique images). Caption: wire the loop's loop_config side output into the Seed List; downstream the prompt list and the seed list pair up by index, so each iteration gets its own seed.
Connecting loop_config auto-matches the seed list's count + strategy to the loop's, so the two lists stay the same length without manual setup. Two other workarounds work too: bake $iteration into the prompt template (the prompt text itself never repeats), or wire $iteration through a WP Var → Int into the sampler's seed input — both fine for simple cases, but the Seed List scales better when you want a deterministic, reproducible series.

sections.title: WP Context Loop
sections.text:
Add a WP Context Loop before your WP Context and one Generate runs the whole chain N times in a single click — each iteration with its own seed and its own fresh roll of your wildcards. The Variation strategy controls how those per-iteration seeds are spread:
Hashed (default)
Each iteration gets an unrelated seed derived from the base. Produces the most variety — neighbouring iterations look nothing alike.
Sequential
Seeds walk seed, seed+1, seed+2 … so adjacent iterations feel related and drift gradually.
Prime stride
Takes large even jumps through the seed space. Good for sampling widely spread results from a known base.
The Override seed toggle on the loop controls whether these strategies apply. When on, the loop derives N seeds from the base and sets each iteration's seed accordingly, making the whole batch reproducible from that one base seed. When off (the default), each downstream Context uses its own widget seed independently and the loop only provides per-iteration variation on top.
To compare chosen options instead of random rolls, use the loop's Sweep combinations menu: it runs every combination of the wildcard options you pick, one iteration each, and can hold everything else steady. See WP Context Loop for details.

sections.title: Per-iteration seed locks
sections.text:
Both WP Context Loop and WP Seed List carry a Per-iteration seeds button that opens a list of the seed each iteration will use. From there you can:
- Lock any single iteration to a fixed seed (the rest stay derived), or Lock all / Unlock all at once.
- Copy / Paste the whole list as #N: seed text to reproduce a series elsewhere — Alt-click Copy grabs only the locked rows.
- Prev — lock the seed an iteration actually used on the previous run, rather than the upcoming one.
Reach for Prev after a run you liked. The list normally shows the seeds for the next run; with control-after-generate set to randomize, the base seed has already rotated, so those upcoming seeds won't reproduce what you just saw. Prev pins the seed that iteration rolled last time — greyed out until a run has happened (and, on the loop, until Override seed is on). So: run once, then lock the iterations worth keeping.

sections.title: Iteration variables
sections.text:
Inside each loop iteration, two variables are available for your templates:
- $iteration — which run you are on, starting at 1 (so 1, 2, 3 … up to the count).
- $iteration_total — the total number of runs, constant across every iteration.
By default both are hidden from the rendered prompt. You can turn off the internal flag for either one in the loop settings if you want them to appear in the output text — for example to label each iteration's output as "frame 1 of 4".
These variables are injected as internal by default, so they will not appear in your prompt unless you deliberately expose them.

sections.title: Turning the loop off
sections.text: The loop has a Bypass switch that collapses it to a single run while keeping the node wired — handy for comparing looped vs single output without rebuilding the graph.

sections.title: Connecting an external seed
sections.text: You can convert the seed widget to an input socket and connect any integer source — a Primitive node, or any other INT output. This lets you synchronise the loop seed with an upstream sampler or another node.

sections.title: Base vs. per-frame
sections.text:
A WP Context Loop fans your chain out into N passes (“frames”). By default every frame resolves from the same module settings — the base. An override is a per-frame exception: a single frame gets a different value while all the others keep using the base. Think of it as a keyframe — most of the run follows the base, and you pin only the spots that need to differ.
Figure: Each frame resolves from the base, then any override recorded for that frame is layered on top. Steps: Base settings (apply to all frames) → default → Frame #k override (patches just frame k) → per-frame patch → Resolved frames (base, except where pinned). Flow diagram of three stages left to right: Base settings (apply to all frames), an arrow labelled default, Frame #k override (patches just frame k), an arrow labelled per-frame patch, and Resolved frames (base, except where pinned). Caption: each frame resolves from the base, then any override recorded for that frame is layered on top, like a keyframe that changes only the frames you pin.

sections.title: Editing a frame
sections.text:
The loop widget carries an edit frame row of chips: base, then #1 #2 #3 … up to the count. Pick a frame chip and the module editors switch to “editing frame #k”: open any module, change it, and the change is recorded as that frame's override — not the base. Switch back to base and you're editing the default that every un-pinned frame uses.
Overrides are sparse: a frame stores only the fields you actually changed, so a four-frame run with one pinned wildcard carries one tiny patch, not four full copies. Each pinned field shows a small badge on its module row so you can see at a glance which frames diverge, and a revert to base control clears a frame's override and returns it to the default.
Overrides are instance-level — they patch how a module resolves for a frame (the pick, the lock, the template text, enable/disable), not its underlying structure. Adding or removing a wildcard option, or changing a module's identity, always edits the base and applies to every frame.

sections.title: What you can override
sections.text:
Wildcard pick
Pin a specific option for one frame while the rest re-roll. Frame #3 always lands on "red"; the others stay random.
Combine template / Fixed value
Give a frame its own template string or fixed value — e.g. a different caption on the last frame.
Constraint reach + matrix tweaks
Adjust a constraint's instance settings for one frame.
Seed lock
Lock a module's seed on one frame only, so just that frame reproduces while the others vary. See the per-frame seed lock below.
Enable / disable
Run a module only on some frames, or skip it on others. See per-frame enable/disable below.

sections.title: Per-frame enable / disable
sections.text:
Every module row has an enable checkbox that's frame-aware. The effective state for a frame is the per-frame setting if you've set one, otherwise the module's base on/off. That makes both directions work:
- Base on, frame off — the module runs everywhere except the frames you switch off.
- Base off, frame on — the module is dormant except on the frames you switch on, so a run can introduce an extra element on just a couple of frames.
A skipped frame still produces an image — the module simply contributes nothing to that pass. In WP Debug a frame turned off by a per-frame switch reads differently from a module that's off at the base, so you can tell intentional per-frame skips from a globally-disabled module.

sections.title: Per-frame seed lock
sections.text:
Seed locks are frame-aware too. Locking a module's seed while a frame chip is active pins the seed for that frame only — the others keep varying. This is the difference between “hold this one element steady across the whole batch” (lock at the base) and “make frame #4 reproducible but let the rest roam” (lock on frame #4). Unlocking a frame whose base is locked records an explicit per-frame unlock, so a single frame can break free of a base lock.
While a frame chip is active, the run-level toggles (Hide from prompt, Hold across run) are disabled — those apply to every frame, so you switch back to base to change them. Only the per-frame things (pick, seed lock, enable) are editable on a frame.

pages.title: Constraints in depth
pages.blurb: Source→target pairing, matrix vs exceptions, one-shot consume.

sections.title: What a constraint does
sections.text:
A Constraint module links a source wildcard to a target wildcard. After the source rolls its pick, the constraint adjusts the target's option pool — boosting some choices, excluding others, or narrowing it to a specific set — before the target rolls. The constraint itself does not set any $variable; it only shapes the odds for the target.
A classic use: the source wildcard picks a season, and the constraint makes warm-toned lighting far more likely when the source rolled "summer", while cool tones become more likely when it rolled "winter".
Figure: Source rolls → constraint adjusts target pool → target rolls. Flow diagram of three boxes left to right. Source wildcard (rolls first) points to Constraint (adjusts target pool), which points to Target wildcard (rolls with adjusted weights). Caption: source rolls, the constraint adjusts the target pool, then the target rolls. It shows the order of events: the source's pick is known before the target rolls, and the constraint only changes the target's odds.

sections.title: Order matters
sections.text: The module stack runs top to bottom. The source wildcard must come before the Constraint, and the Constraint must come before the target wildcard. A constraint whose source has not yet rolled is silently skipped for that iteration.

sections.title: Matrix and exceptions
sections.text:
A constraint's rules come in two layers that work together:
- Matrix — rules that apply to whole subcategory pairs. For example: when source subcategory "season/warm" rolled, boost all target options in subcategory "lighting/warm".
- Exceptions — rules that apply to specific individual option pairs. These override the matrix for exact combinations.
When a matrix rule and an exception both match a given pair, the exception wins. This lets you set broad subcategory behaviour and then fine-tune individual combinations on top.
Each rule has a mode:
Allow
No change. Shown as Neutral in the matrix: the pair rolls as if there were no rule.
Exclude
Remove matching options from the target pool before it rolls.
Boost
Multiply the weight of matching options by the factor you set (> 1 = more likely).
Reduce
Multiply the weight of matching options by a factor less than 1 (= less likely).
Only
Link picks. When the source rolls this, only targets that have a rule of their own in the same row can be picked. Everything else in the row is removed.
Figure: The SPA's full Edit constraint page for the Starter pairing entry (breadcrumb Library › Constraints › Starter pairing, Unsaved badge). Wildcards section pins Starter subject as source + Starter mood as target. Rule matrix grids feline/canine × calm/intense with feline×intense + canine×calm at ↑×3 and the mismatched diagonals at ↓×0.3. Exceptions table below carries one row: tiger → sleepy · Exclude · — — the EXTRA exception wins over the matrix when both apply. Screenshot of the manager's Edit constraint page for Starter pairing (breadcrumb Library › Constraints › Starter pairing, with an Unsaved badge), with the library sidebar on the left. The Wildcards section picks Starter subject as Source wildcard (rows of the matrix) and Starter mood as Target wildcard (columns). The Rule matrix crosses the source sub-categories feline and canine with the target sub-categories calm and intense: feline × intense and canine × calm are boosted ×3, feline × calm and canine × intense are reduced ×0.3. Below, Exceptions (1) holds one row, source value tiger, target value sleepy, mode Exclude, and the page ends with Delete, Cancel and Save.

sections.title: Linking picks with Only
sections.text:
Only ties one wildcard's pick to another's. Add an exception maid → frilled apron in Only mode, and whenever the source rolls "maid" the target can only roll "frilled apron". You don't list every outfit to exclude, and an outfit you add to the target later is shut out too.
- On an exception, Only links exact values. Several Only exceptions for the same source value make a short list: "maid" can pick "frilled apron" or "kimono" and nothing else. A target with any other exception of its own for that source (a Boost, say) stays in the pool with that rule.
- In the matrix, Only links subcategories. An Only cell summer → open means a summer pick can only reach targets tagged open (or tagged with anything else that has a rule in the summer row). The other cells in that row show a faint × so you can see what is shut out. A Neutral cell does not count as a rule here.
Only rows and exceptions for other source values are unaffected. A "biker" pick in the example above still rolls every outfit.

sections.title: Accepts axes as a source or target
sections.text:
When a wildcard group is marked accepts — an axis, read as $var.AXIS — the matrix folds differently on whichever side of the constraint the axis sits, so the tag you read always agrees with the tag the constraint acts on.
- Accepts source. The axis rolls exactly one tag per pick, so the constraint keys on that single rolled tag — not every tag the source option carries. A source outfit tagged sneakers · heels · sandals that rolls sandals makes a diagonal “same tag wins” matrix pin the target to sandals, so $outfit.SHOES and the shoe that gets picked match. A classify source keeps the older behaviour: all its tags apply together (AND), so a multi-tag classify option under a strict diagonal can exclude the whole target pool.
- Accepts target. A target option's tags inside an accepts axis are alternatives, so the option stays in the pool when the source allows any of them, and the target's own axis roll is then restricted to the allowed tag. A target shoe tagged sandals · heels isn't dropped just because heels is excluded — it survives as sandals and rolls sandals.
Put the two together — an accepts source, an accepts target, and a diagonal matrix — and $source.AXIS always equals $target.AXIS: the two wildcards agree on the axis every run.

sections.title: Target reach
sections.text:
A constraint is not a one-shot. By default it re-weights every target wildcard instance it can reach downstream — including instances reached through nested @{uuid} refs. The per-instance Target reach selector lets you narrow that scope when re-weighting every match is too broad:
All
Default. Re-weight every target instance the constraint can reach downstream — direct rows and instances reached through nested refs alike.
First
Re-weight only the first reachable target instance; every later one rolls unconstrained.
Next N
Re-weight the next N reachable instances (you set the count, minimum 1); the rest roll unconstrained.
Pick
Re-weight only the instances you tick from a checklist of reachable targets — direct rows, or nested-ref carrier options that resolve to the target.
Reach is always measured downstream of the constraint: it can only see — and count toward First / Next N — target instances that come after it in the run. A Pick selection names each instance the same way the engine matches it: a direct row by its per-instance id, or a nested ref by its carrier row plus the option that hosts the @{uuid}.
If a constraint's reach covers zero reachable targets — its only target sits above it, the count overshoots what's downstream, or a picked instance no longer exists — it is flagged constraint_orphan_target so a dead pairing surfaces instead of silently doing nothing. Separately, a constraint that reaches fewer instances than a Next N / Pick selector asked for is noted as a partial reach.
A constraint can also rule out every option of its target for some source value (each one excluded, shut out by an Only rule, or weighted 0). If the target has no fallback it would come out empty, so the constraint row gets a rules out all badge before you run; hover it to see which source values do it. Allow an option for those values, or mark one of the target's options as its fallback.
You can still add multiple Constraint modules for the same source→target pair — one per distinct rule — and give each its own reach. Stack position plus each module's reach decide which instances every constraint claims.

sections.title: Constraints reach through nested refs
sections.text: If the target wildcard appears only inside another wildcard's option text (via a @{uuid} nested reference), the constraint still applies — it follows the reference chain to find the target. Each such reachable instance counts as one target for the reach selector above, and a Pick entry can name it by its carrier row plus the hosting option. A safeguard counts each downstream instance only once even when multiple reference paths converge on it.

sections.title: When a source or target is missing
sections.text: A constraint refers to its source and target wildcards by id. If one isn't in your library — you installed the constraint without its wildcards, or deleted one — that axis is stranded: the editor shows the dead id with its remembered name and keeps the rule matrix read-only until you heal it. Reattach re-points the axis at a local wildcard (or downloads the missing one from the community), then remaps the matrix and exceptions onto the new wildcard's sub-categories.

pages.title: Internal variables
pages.blurb: Hide a $var from the rendered prompt; when it's stripped.

sections.title: What internal means
sections.text:
When you mark a module as internal in its settings, all the variables it produces are hidden from the final rendered prompt. They still travel through the whole pipeline — you can read them in combine and derivation modules further down the chain — but they are removed just before the Assembler turns the template into text, so they never appear in the output.
A typical use: a wildcard picks a lighting key code like $_lighting_key, marked internal. A derivation module then uses that key to produce a human-readable $lighting description. Only the description reaches the prompt; the key code stays hidden.

sections.title: Internal variables survive chaining
sections.text:
Internal variables are only removed at the render step inside the Assembler — not when a Context passes its output to the next node. This means a variable set as internal in Context A is still readable by a derivation in Context B downstream. Only the final Assembler hides it from the prompt.
You can set a variable internal in an early Context and use it as a building block in every subsequent Context in the chain — it will never pollute your rendered prompt.

sections.title: Loop iteration variable flags
sections.text: The $iteration and $iteration_total variables injected by WP Context Loop each have their own internal flag in the loop configuration. By default both are internal, so they do not show up in the rendered prompt. Turn off the flag for either one if you want it to appear — for example, to caption outputs with "frame 1 of 4".

pages.title: Negatives
pages.blurb: Send words to the negative prompt from the option, value or rule that needs them.

sections.title: The idea
sections.text:
A negative belongs to the $variable it came with, and only reaches an Assembler that actually uses that variable. The main Assembler that renders $hair, $mood and $face gets all three variables' negative words; a face detailer Assembler that only renders $face gets only the face words from the same Context.
Figure: Negatives follow usage: words only reach a negative output when their variable was rendered. Steps: Wildcard option (negative: fruit) → picked → $hair (carries it) → used → Assembler (renders $hair) → collected → negative output (fruit). Flow diagram of four stages left to right: a Wildcard option carrying 'negative: fruit', an arrow labelled picked, the variable $hair (carries it), an arrow labelled used, the Assembler (renders $hair), an arrow labelled collected, and the negative output (fruit). Caption: negatives follow usage, so words only reach an Assembler's negative output when their variable was rendered by its template.

sections.title: Where negatives come from
sections.text:
Wildcard option
Each option has an optional Negative line under its value. When that option is picked, its words attach to the wildcard's $variable. A multi-pick attaches each picked option's words to its own pick. The null option has no negative.
Fixed value
Each value has the same Negative line. A fixed value always applies, so its negative travels with the variable wherever it is used. Handy for style presets: $style brings “photo, 3d render” along with it. On a Context node (and in the bundle editor) each row shows its negative under the value: change it there for that use only, clear it, or add one to a row you added; the reset button brings back the library's.
Combine
A combine carries the negatives of every variable its template read, with no setup. On top of that it has one optional Negative of its own, for words that belong to the phrase as a whole. Like its template, that negative can be changed on a Context node or in the bundle editor for that use only, with a reset button to go back to the library's.
Derivation “Add to negative”
A fourth action next to Replace, Append and Prepend. It leaves the target variable's text alone and adds the value to that variable's negatives, so a rule like “when $mood is gloomy, add ‘smiling’” follows $mood wherever it goes. With + And, one branch can replace a variable and add to its negative in the same step. “Replace negative” is the fifth action: it drops the variable's negative words and uses the value instead.
Context Injector row
Socket rows and template rows can carry a Negative, written with the same $slot grammar as the row template. It replaces whatever negatives the variable carried before, so injecting $character over a picked one swaps the pick's negative for the row's.

sections.title: What each negative field accepts
sections.text:
A negative field takes the same syntax as the value field next to it.
Field | Accepts
Wildcard option negative | text, {a|b}, @{ref} (no $vars)
Fixed value negative | text, {a|b} (no refs, no $vars)
Combine negative | $vars, {a|b}
Derivation “Add to negative” value | $vars, @{ref}, {a|b}
Injector row negative | the row's $input_N slots, like the row template
Assembler negative template | $vars and the reserved $negatives slot
Negatives never change your picks. Negative text rolls on its own seed stream, and an @{ref} inside a negative resolves quietly: it doesn't count as a pick, isn't logged in the Test Runner trace, doesn't trigger constraints, and the picked option's own negative is ignored. Adding or editing a negative leaves every seed's prompt exactly as it was.

sections.title: How they follow the variable
sections.text:
A write replaces, an append keeps
When a module writes a variable, the old value's negatives go with it. A derivation Replace swaps them for the negatives of whatever its new text read; Append and Prepend keep the old ones and add the new.
Index and axis accessors
$props.0 carries only the first pick's negative. Bare $props and $props.AXIS carry every pick's.
Internal variables add nothing
An internal variable never renders in a prompt, so its negatives never reach a negative output, even though they are kept for downstream modules that read it.
Variables in the negative template
A $var you write in the Assembler's negative template adds its text, not its own negatives.
Reading a variable's negatives: $name.neg
$pose.neg is the negative words $pose carries at that point in the chain, and $props.1.neg only pick 1's. It works wherever $vars do: hand one variable's negatives to another with “Add to negative” and the value $pose_portrait.neg, use it in a combine or the Assembler's negative template, or test it in a condition. Reading .neg is not a use of $pose, so it never pulls $pose's words in a second time.

sections.title: The Assembler's negative output
sections.text:
WP Prompt Assembler has a second output, negative, next to prompt. Wire it into your negative CLIP Text Encode. Under the preview sits a collapsible negative template:
- $negatives marks where the collected words go, e.g. lowres, bad anatomy, $negatives.
- An empty template outputs just the collected words.
- A template without $negatives gets the collected words appended at the end.
Repeated tags are dropped (case-insensitive, and (blurry:1.2) counts as blurry), including tags you already typed in the template.

sections.title: Cleaning both prompts
sections.text: WP Prompt Cleaner takes an optional negative input and returns a cleaned negative output beside the prompt. Its rule list has a second column for the negative: it follows the prompt column's preset, except fuzzy dedupe and the blocklist are off. The extra rule Drop negative tags also in prompt (off by default) removes a tag from the negative when the prompt asks for it too; either way the report names the overlap.

sections.title: Bulk add
sections.text:
In a wildcard's bulk add, -- starts an option's negative. Everything after the first -- is the negative, and #tag / *N still work at the end of either side:
Module | Line
Wildcard | strawberry blonde #warm *2 -- strawberry, fruit
Fixed values | style = oil painting -- photo, 3d render
With options checked, bulk edit's Negative menu adds words to each checked option, replaces their negative, or clears it.

sections.title: Seeing where each word came from
sections.text: WP Debug lists a variable's negative words under its value, naming the module when they came from elsewhere (a derivation's Add to negative, a combine inheriting from $hair). The Test Runner shows a NEG line under each output, tinted by the variable each word came from, adds a Negative column to Samples, and Compare lists a seed whose negative changed.

sections.title: Sharing
sections.text: A module or bundle that uses a negative (or an “Add to negative” action) is stamped schema 8 when you publish it. Older versions of the extension refuse schema 8 packs and ask you to update, instead of silently dropping the negatives. Injector rows and Cleaner settings live in the workflow, not the library, so they need no schema bump.

pages.title: Conflicts & warnings
pages.blurb: The advisory scanner + runtime warnings (never blocks).

sections.title: Where you'll see them
sections.text:
You never have to go looking — problems come to you in two places:
- On the node, while you build — the WP Context shows small coloured dots with a short label (e.g. a duplicate variable, a missing one). Hover any dot for the full, plain-English message. A Subgraph that contains WP nodes gets a single badge summarising the worst issue inside it, so you can spot trouble without opening it.
- In WP Debug, after a run — open the Warnings tab on a WP Debug node to see what came up during the actual generation, in order, one line each.
Figure: A three-node chain showing both sides of the warning system. WP Context (Starter subject + Starter style + Starter pairing, the pairing row outlined in amber with a TGT MISSING badge because its target wildcard isn't in the chain) → WP Debug with the Warnings tab open on CONSTRAINT_NEVER_APPLIED → WP Prompt Assembler still resolving 'A picture of a cat, in the style of oil painting'. Warnings are advisory; the run carries on. Screenshot of a three-node chain. A WP Context holds Starter subject, Starter style and Starter pairing; the Starter pairing constraint row is outlined in amber with a TGT MISSING badge because its target wildcard is not in the chain. It feeds a WP Debug with the Warnings tab open (1 warning), showing CONSTRAINT_NEVER_APPLIED: the constraint @Starter pairing did not apply because no @mood wildcard instance or nested-ref carrier was found in this chain. Last, a WP Prompt Assembler with template 'A picture of a $subject, in the style of $style' still resolves to 'A picture of a cat, in the style of oil painting'. Warnings are advisory; the run carries on.

sections.title: Reading the colour
sections.text:
The dot's colour tells you how much to care — the wording in the hover message tells you exactly what:
- Blue (info) — just so you know. Usually nothing to fix (an intended override, a constraint that didn't come up).
- Amber (warning) — worth a look. Something probably isn't doing what you meant (a duplicate, a missing variable, a mis-ordered constraint).
- Red — something won't resolve as written (a reference that points nowhere). The run still completes; that piece just won't take effect.
Every flag here is advisory. It never blocks generation or raises an error. Writing a variable twice is perfectly valid — the later write wins; the dot just makes the override visible so it's a choice, not an accident.

sections.title: Common things it flags
sections.text:
Shadowed variable
An earlier WP Context already sets this variable and yours overrides it. Normal when you chain Contexts — it's shown (as info, not a warning) so the override is on purpose, not a surprise.
Duplicate variable
Two modules in the same Context produce the same variable. The lower one wins. Rename one, or reorder them if the wrong value is coming through.
Missing variable
Your Prompt Assembler template uses a $variable that nothing upstream produces — it resolves to empty (the canvas preview underlines the token so you can spot it). Add a module that sets it, or drop the token.
Constraint not wired
A constraint can't find one of its two wildcards, or they're in the wrong order — the constraint has to sit between its source and target wildcard to fire.
Constraint never fired
A constraint was set up correctly but its target wildcard never came up on this run, so it had no effect. Often fine — just letting you know it didn't do anything.
That's the short list. The Warning & conflict types reference page has the full set with what each one means and what to do about it.

pages.title: Bundles
pages.blurb: Group + reuse modules; frozen snapshots; enable overlay.

sections.title: What a bundle is
sections.text:
A bundle groups a contiguous range of modules in a Context into a named, collapsible unit. You can collapse it in the module stack to keep long setups tidy, and you can save it to the library to reuse the whole group in other Contexts or workflows.
At generation time the bundle is transparent — its modules run inline exactly as if they had been placed directly in the stack. The bundle is purely an organisational tool; it does not add any processing of its own.
Figure: Three nodes side-by-side. Left WP Context shows the Starter set bundle expanded — six child rows (Starter subject, pairing, mood, style, scene, accent) nested under the bundle frame. Middle WP Context shows the same bundle COLLAPSED into a single row. Right WP Prompt Assembler reads the resolved $vars from either Context the same way — the bundle is transparent at runtime. Screenshot of three canvas nodes. On the left a WP Context shows the Starter set bundle expanded, its six child rows nested inside the bundle frame: Starter subject, Starter pairing, Starter mood, Starter style, Starter scene and Starter accent. In the middle a second WP Context holds the same Starter set bundle collapsed to one row (6 mods), feeding a WP Prompt Assembler on the right. The assembler's template is '$scene, $style, $accent, masterpiece, highly detailed', with chips $style, $scene and $accent, and the preview resolves to 'dramatic cat, oil painting, cinematic lighting, masterpiece, highly detailed'. Expanded or collapsed, a bundle publishes the same $variables.

sections.title: Frozen snapshots
sections.text:
When you capture a bundle, the current state of each module — its options, settings, and metadata — is saved into the bundle as a frozen snapshot. Changes you later make to the source modules in the library do not propagate into existing bundles. Each bundle keeps resolving from the state it captured.
Because bundle children are frozen, deleting a source wildcard from the library does not break bundles that captured it. The bundle keeps working. A MISSING badge appears on the workflow row to signal that the library entry and the bundle's snapshot have diverged — giving you an honest indication to decide whether to update or leave it as-is.

sections.title: Disabling a bundle
sections.text: Each bundle has an enabled toggle. Disabling a bundle suppresses all its children without touching their individual settings. Re-enabling it restores them exactly as they were. This lets you mute an entire group of modules in one click during testing without having to disable each one separately.

sections.title: Inserting a bundle
sections.text: When you drop a saved bundle into a Context, each child module receives a fresh ID so that inserting the same bundle multiple times does not cause ID collisions. Any @{uuid} references and constraint pairings inside the bundle are automatically rewritten to match the new IDs.

sections.title: Bundles are not a module kind
sections.text: Bundles are a grouping and portability mechanism, not a processing step. They have no module type, no kind colour, and no engine handler of their own. Everything they contribute to the pipeline comes from their children.

pages.title: WP Context
pages.blurb: Rolls a module stack into a $variable Context.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
A WP Context is where you define the named values that power your prompt. Add a wildcard module and it becomes $subject. Add a fixed-value module and it becomes $style. When you press Generate the node rolls every module with your seed and hands a complete map of $variable → value to whatever is wired downstream.
Chain two Context nodes together — the downstream one can add new variables or override ones set above. The last write wins, so a downstream $subject replaces the upstream one.
Figure: A WP Context with three modules in its stack (Starter subject wildcard, Starter scene combine flagged orange MISSING VAR because $mood isn't published, Starter style fixed) wired into a WP Prompt Assembler. The assembler chip strip lists the three upstream $vars; the resolved preview shows 'cat, oil painting,, masterpiece, highly detailed' — the empty slot where $scene would have rendered makes the missing-var warning concrete. Screenshot of a WP Context (seed 42, fixed, modules 3 / 3) wired into a WP Prompt Assembler. The Context stack holds Starter subject, Starter scene and Starter style; the Starter scene row is outlined in amber with a MISSING VAR badge because a variable it reads is not published. The assembler's template is '$scene, $style,, masterpiece, highly detailed', its chip strip lists $subject, $scene and $style as 3 upstream, and the preview resolves to 'cat, oil painting,, masterpiece, highly detailed'. It shows the Context's module stack and how a missing-variable warning appears on a row.

sections.title: Inputs & outputs
sections.text:
upstream (in)
Connect an earlier WP Context here to chain them together. Its variables flow through and can be overridden by modules in this node. Leave unconnected to start a fresh chain.
seed
Controls the random picks inside this node. Change it to get a different roll; right-click → Convert widget to input to drive it from a seed widget or the WP Context Loop.
modules
The stack of modules inside this node — wildcards, fixed values, combines, constraints, and bundles. Add modules by clicking the + button. Drag rows to reorder.
context (out)
The resolved variable map produced by this node. Wire it into a WP Prompt Assembler, WP Debug, WP Context Injector, or another WP Context.

sections.title: Per-module behaviour in a loop
sections.text:
When a WP Context Loop drives this node, each module chooses how it behaves across the batch through its Runtime settings:
- Hold across run — the module resolves once at the first frame and reuses that exact value on every frame of the run (the resolved value, not just the seed — constrained picks and nested @{} refs stay frozen too), then re-rolls next run. The “keep this element steady for the whole batch” switch. Flip it from the module's Runtime settings, or right-click the row and pick Hold across run for a two-click toggle.
- Per-frame overrides — using the loop's edit frame selector you can give one frame its own pick, seed lock, or enable/disable for any module in the stack, leaving the rest of the batch on the base.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
Lock a module's seed (via the module's instance options) to freeze that pick across all WP Context Loop iterations — handy for holding the art style steady while the subject varies across a batch.
Modules you add to a WP Context are snapshots, not live links. If you edit a module in the library afterward, the Context doesn't change under you — it flags that row as drifted so you can pull (sync) the updated version when you're ready. That keeps a saved workflow reproducible: it won't silently change because you edited a module somewhere else.

pages.title: WP Context Loop
pages.blurb: Emit N Contexts so the chain auto-iterates.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
Normally one Generate runs the whole chain once — one WP Context, one resolved prompt. Put a WP Context Loop in front of your WP Context and a single Generate re-runs the chain N times instead, re-rolling your wildcards each pass, so one click yields N different Contexts and prompts (and whatever your sampler renders downstream from each). Set the count to 8, press Generate once, and compare eight variations. No repeated queueing, no batch node to wire.
Figure: WP Context Loop (seed 42 fixed, count 4, hash strategy, $iteration var) → WP Context (Starter subject + Starter style) → WP Prompt Assembler with template '$iteration of $iteration_total: A picture of a $subject, in the style of $style' → Show Any. Show Any prints four numbered lines side-by-side: '1 of 4: A picture of a cat, in the style of oil painting', dog, dog, wolf — one resolved prompt per loop pass before the chain hands them downstream to a sampler. Screenshot of a four-node loop chain. WP Context Loop (seed 42, fixed, count 4, strategy hash, iteration var $iteration) feeds a WP Context holding Starter subject and Starter style, which feeds a WP Prompt Assembler with template '$iteration of $iteration_total: A picture of a $subject, in the style of $style' and chips $iteration, $iteration_total, $subject and $style. A Show Any node on the right prints four lines: '1 of 4: A picture of a cat, in the style of oil painting', then dog, dog and wolf for 2, 3 and 4 of 4. It shows the loop producing one resolved prompt per pass.

sections.title: The controls
sections.text:
Count
How many variations to make in one run (1–999). Set it to 1 to switch looping off without removing the node.
Seed
The starting point for the batch. Change it for a different set of variations; keep it the same to reproduce the same batch. Right-click → Convert widget to input to drive it from another seed node.
Override seed
On: the loop chooses the seed for every iteration, so the whole batch is reproducible from this one seed. Off (default): each WP Context keeps using its own seed and the loop just nudges it per iteration.
Variation strategy
How the per-iteration seeds spread out. Hashed (default) makes each iteration unrelated and maximally varied; Sequential walks seed, seed+1, seed+2… so neighbours feel related; Prime stride takes large even jumps.
Bypass
The node's own on/off switch. When on, the loop collapses to a single run but stays wired, so you can flip it back without rebuilding the graph.

sections.title: Per-iteration control
sections.text:
Two more controls open finer, per-iteration tuning of the batch:
- Per-iteration seeds — the seed list for the run. Lock individual iterations, Lock all / Unlock all, Copy / Paste the series as #N: seed text, or Prev to lock the seed an iteration actually used on the previous run. These locks take effect when Override seed is on.
- Edit frame — the base / #1 #2 … chip row. Pick a frame and the module editors switch to editing just that frame, recording a per-frame override — a pinned wildcard pick, a tweaked template, a per-frame seed lock, or a per-frame enable/disable. base edits the default every un-pinned frame uses.

sections.title: Sweep combinations
sections.text:
Open Sweep combinations from the loop node and switch it on to compare options side by side instead of rolling them. Pick one or more wildcards from the WP Context nodes after the loop, choose which of their options to include, and the loop runs every combination, one frame each. Sweep $hair (3 options) against $mood (2 options) and a single Generate makes 6 frames: red + calm, red + sad, blue + calm, and so on. The menu shows the total and lists every frame before you run, the node's button shows the frame count, and the count widget follows it. Above each wildcard's options, all ticks every option, none clears them so you can tick just the few you want, and enabled only goes back to the options enabled in the wildcard. A wildcard with nothing ticked sweeps nothing until you tick one.
- Order — the first wildcard changes slowest and the last one fastest, so a two-wildcard sweep reads like a grid: one row per option of the first, one column per option of the second. Use the arrow to reorder.
- Limit — the most frames a sweep runs (64 by default, up to 999). When the combinations outnumber it, the loop runs the first ones in order and says so.
- Hold other picks (on by default) — everything you are not sweeping keeps the same pick on every frame, so the only thing that changes is what you swept. Turn it off to let the rest re-roll per frame as in a normal loop.
Each frame pins the swept wildcards exactly like pinning an option by hand, so their tag axes still roll and constraints they drive still apply downstream. A swept wildcard is not itself re-weighted by constraints, because the sweep decides its pick. Frame bypass and per-frame overrides work as usual. Changing the sweep moves each seed lock and bypassed frame with its combination, and drops it when that combination no longer runs; lowering the count drops the ones past it.
For a clean comparison, keep the sampler on one fixed seed (a plain KSampler already does), so the image only changes where the prompt does.

sections.title: Iteration variables
sections.text:
Each run, the loop hands you two variables to drop into your prompt template or any combine:
- $iteration — which run you're on, starting at 1 (1, 2, 3 … up to the count). Handy for labelling outputs.
- $iteration_total — the total number of runs. Same on every iteration.
For example, a template of frame $iteration of $iteration_total — $subject renders “frame 1 of 4 — a fox”, “frame 2 of 4 — a cat”, and so on. These two variables stay out of the rendered prompt by default — switch their internal flag off in the loop config if you want them to appear in the text.
Figure: The full looped workflow rendered: WP Context Loop + WP Context + WP Prompt Assembler feed a KSampler whose seeds come from a WP Seed List on the loop's config, and a second assembler ('iteration $iteration of $iteration_total') drives an Add Text Overlay. The result is a 2×2 grid of four portraits (a dog, a cat, a dog, a wolf) labelled 'iteration 1 of 4' through 'iteration 4 of 4': one image per pass, each with its own prompt and seed. Screenshot of a full looped workflow and its output. WP Context Loop (count 4, hash) feeds a WP Context with Starter subject and Starter style and a WP Prompt Assembler ('A picture of a $subject, in the style of $style'),. The loop's loop_config also feeds a WP Seed List whose seeds go to a KSampler with CLIP Text Encode (Prompt) and VAE Decode; a second assembler with template 'iteration $iteration of $iteration_total' drives an Add Text Overlay. The Preview Image shows a 2 by 2 grid of painted animal portraits captioned iteration 1 of 4 to iteration 4 of 4: a dog, a cat, a dog and a wolf. One image per pass, each with its own prompt and seed.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
A module with a locked seed ignores the loop — it makes the same pick every iteration. Useful for holding one thing steady (say, the art style) while everything else varies across the batch.
The loop emits a list of prompts — one per iteration. Downstream samplers run once per prompt, but a standard KSampler takes a single seed (not a list), so every iteration is sampled with that same seed. If two iterations happen to roll the exact same prompt string (e.g. your wildcards landed on the same options twice), the sampler produces the same image for both. Three ways to keep every output distinct:
- Drop a WP Seed List between the loop and your sampler (cleanest). It emits a list of N seeds — one per iteration — that pairs with the loop's prompts so each (prompt, seed) combination is unique. Wire its loop_config input from the loop's side output and it auto-matches the loop's count + strategy.
- Bake $iteration into the prompt template — it never repeats, so the prompt text is always unique.
- Wire $iteration through a WP Var → Int into the sampler's seed input so each iteration also gets its own seed.

pages.title: WP Seed List
pages.blurb: Emit N derived seeds — one per loop iteration — for downstream samplers.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
A standard KSampler takes a single INT seed. When a WP Context Loop emits N prompts, the sampler runs N times but reads the same seed every pass — so two iterations that happen to roll the exact same prompt string would produce the exact same image. Drop a WP Seed List between the loop and your sampler: it emits a list of N derived seeds, pairing one with each prompt, so every iteration gets its own (prompt, seed) combo.
The node works standalone too — even without a loop wired in, the widget controls produce a stable, reproducible series of N seeds you can fan out across any node that accepts INT.

sections.title: The controls
sections.text:
Base seed
The starting point for the seed series. Change it for a different batch of seeds; keep it the same to reproduce the same set. Right-click → Convert widget to input to drive it from another seed node.
Count
How many seeds to emit in one run (1–999). When you wire a WP Context Loop into loop_config, the count auto-mirrors the loop's count so the two lists stay the same length.
Strategy
How the per-iteration seeds are spread out — Hashed (default), Sequential (base, base+1, base+2 …), or Stride (large prime jumps). Picks a chip inside the node's DOM widget.
Override base seed from loop
When ON and loop_config is wired, the node uses the loop's base seed instead of the local widget. Independent of the count + strategy toggles so you can mix sources.
Override count from loop
When ON and loop_config is wired, the node uses the loop's count. Auto-flips ON the moment you connect a loop_config wire — flip it off manually if you want a different count.
Override strategy from loop
When ON and loop_config is wired, the node uses the loop's strategy. Also auto-flips ON when you connect the wire.
loop_config (in)
Optional WP Context Loop side-output. Wire it in to have the seed series mirror the loop's shape automatically.
seed (out)
List of N derived seeds — one per iteration. Connect it to a KSampler's seed input (or anything that takes INT) and the downstream node fans out across the series in lockstep with the loop's prompts.

sections.title: The flow with WP Context Loop
sections.text:
Figure: The loop's side-output drives the seed list's count + strategy; the loop's prompt list and the seed list pair up one-to-one downstream so every iteration gets a unique seed. Steps: WP Context Loop (N prompts) → loop_config → WP Seed List (N seeds) → paired by index → KSampler (N unique images). Flow diagram of three nodes left to right: WP Context Loop (N prompts), an arrow labelled loop_config, WP Seed List (N seeds), an arrow labelled paired by index, and KSampler (N unique images). Caption: the loop's side output drives the seed list's count and strategy; the loop's prompt list and the seed list pair up one to one downstream, so every iteration gets a unique seed.
Wire the loop's loop_config side-output into the seed list's loop_config input and the override-count + override-strategy toggles auto-flip ON. From that point on the seed series matches the loop's length and shape without you touching the widgets. Flip Override base seed from loop on as well if you want the loop's base seed to anchor the series too; leave it off to keep a different sampler base.
Disconnecting the loop_config wire leaves the override toggles where they are — the widget values stay as the fallback so the node keeps running standalone. Re-connecting the wire auto-arms the toggles again.

sections.title: Variation strategies
sections.text:
Same three strategies as WP Context Loop, applied to the seed series instead of per-iteration Context seeds:
- Hashed (default) — each iteration gets an unrelated seed derived from the base. Most variety; recommended.
- Sequential — base, base+1, base+2 … Adjacent iterations feel related and drift gradually.
- Stride — large prime jumps through the seed space. Wide spread, deterministic.
Every emitted seed is masked to 50 bits so it stays inside the range ComfyUI's frontend produces when you press the seed randomise button — you can copy any seed back into a standalone sampler and it'll reproduce identically.

sections.title: Per-iteration seed locks
sections.text:
The Per-iteration seeds button opens the seed list, where you can pin any iteration to a fixed seed while the rest stay derived — handy for keeping a couple of results you liked while the others keep exploring. Lock all / Unlock all, Copy / Paste (as #N: seed text), and a per-row Prev button round it out.
Prev locks the seed an iteration actually used on the previous run, not the upcoming one — the right choice when control-after-generate is randomising the base. The Seed List captures its series on every run, so Prev lights up after the first generate.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
The seed list pairs with the loop by list index, not by any wire-based handshake. As long as the counts match (which the auto-on override guarantees when you wire loop_config), iteration N's prompt always gets paired with seed N.
Without a loop wired in, the seed list still emits N seeds — useful for fanning a single sampler out N ways from one click. But if you connect it to a non-loop chain that expects a single seed, ComfyUI will iterate the downstream node N times anyway. Set the count to 1 to collapse to single-seed behaviour without removing the node.

pages.title: WP Context Injector
pages.blurb: Lift external node outputs into named $vars.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
Most variables in the pipeline come from wildcards and fixed values inside a WP Context. The WP Context Injector lets you bring in values from outside — a LoRA name picked by another node, an INT from a seed widget, a FLOAT from a slider — and give each one a $variable name. From that point on it behaves just like any other variable: you can reference it in the Assembler template, use it in a Combine rule, or read it in a Derivation.
Chain multiple injectors for more bindings. Each one passes the upstream Context through unchanged and adds its own variables on top.
Figure: A String (Multiline) node feeding a long template into WP Context Injector. The injector widget shows two binding rows (template_subject + subject) wired to the multiline String output. Its context output flows into WP Prompt Assembler ($subject variable chip lit) and a Show Any node renders the assembled prompt downstream. Screenshot of a canvas chain feeding outside text into the pipeline. Two String (Multiline) nodes on the left, one with character tags (ochako uraraka, brown hair, brown eyes…) and one with clothing tags (skirt, sleeveless, sweater, turtleneck…), wire into input_0 and input_1 of a WP Context Injector. Its injected variables list (3 / 3) names input_0 as $lora_subject, input_1 as $lora_clothes, and a template row sets $subject to '$lora_subject wearing $lora_clothes'. The injector's context feeds a WP Prompt Assembler whose template is just $subject, and a Show Any node on the right prints the combined text. It shows how outside node outputs become named $variables.

sections.title: The flow
sections.text: Figure: The injector lifts an outside value into a named $variable the rest of the pipeline can use. Steps: External node (any output) → wire → WP Context Injector (names it $var) → $variable → WP Context (merged in). Flow diagram of three stages left to right: External node (any output), an arrow labelled wire, WP Context Injector (names it $var), an arrow labelled $variable, and WP Context (merged in). Caption: the injector lifts an outside value into a named $variable the rest of the pipeline can use.

sections.title: Ports & sockets
sections.text:
upstream (in)
An existing Context to extend. All of its variables pass through; the injector adds or overrides bindings on top. Leave unconnected to create a standalone Context from injected values only.
rows widget
Holds two kinds of rows: socket rows (one per wired input) and template rows you add manually. Each defines one $variable and can be marked internal (available to modules but hidden from the final prompt).
input_0 … input_9
Dynamic socket slots. Wire any ComfyUI output — a STRING, INT, FLOAT, or anything else — into a slot. A socket row appears automatically. Add up to 10 sockets; chain a second injector for more.
context (out)
The upstream Context with your injected bindings merged on top. Wire it into an Assembler, Debug node, or another Context.

sections.title: Two kinds of rows
sections.text:
The injector resolves rows top to bottom in two passes. Socket rows run first — each one turns a single wired input into a $variable, and its template (if any) can only reference its own socket. Template rows run last, so they can compose from every input and from the variables the socket rows produced.
Socket row
Created automatically when you wire an input, and removed when you disconnect it. Binds that one socket to a $variable. Its optional template may reference only its OWN socket (e.g. the input_0 row can use $input_0) — rows resolve top to bottom, so a socket row can't read a later socket.
Template row
Add one with the “Add template row” button. It isn't tied to any socket and survives disconnects. It runs after all socket rows, so its template can compose from both the raw sockets ($input_0, $input_1, …) and the variables the socket rows produced ($test). Use it to combine multiple inputs.

sections.title: Row options
sections.text:
Binding name
The $variable name that downstream modules and the Assembler will see. Use letters, digits, and underscores; must start with a letter.
Template
On a socket row: leave blank to write the raw socket value as-is, or wrap just that socket (e.g. prefix $input_0). On a template row: required — compose from any input or socket-row variable (e.g. $input_0 by $test). Use $$ for a literal dollar sign.
Negative
Optional, on both row kinds, under Template in the row's edit panel. Negative words for this $variable, written with the same $slot grammar as the template, so a wired string (say, the negative an LLM node writes) can feed it. They replace whatever negatives the variable carried before, and reach only Assemblers that render the variable. A row with a negative shows a NEG badge.
Internal
Tick this to make the variable available to Combine and Derivation modules downstream but keep it out of the assembled prompt text. Works on both row kinds.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
To combine two sockets without an extra Combine module, click Add template row and set a template like $input_0 by $input_1. You name the row's $variable inline in its header and set that template from the row's edit panel (right-click the row → Edit) — the same edit panel socket rows use. A template row runs after every socket row, so it can also reference the variables those rows produce (for example $test) — and it sticks around even if you re-wire the inputs. A socket row's own template can only use its own socket.
A row's negative follows the usual rule: it only reaches an Assembler that renders the row's variable. An internal row, or a boolean that only feeds a derivation, never adds to a negative output. Injector rows live in the workflow, so a negative here needs no library schema bump.
The injector is best suited for STRING, INT, and FLOAT values. Complex types like IMAGE or LATENT are stored as their text representation, which is rarely useful in a prompt.

pages.title: WP Model Info
pages.blurb: Name the loaded checkpoint so rules can branch on it.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
One prompt setup rarely suits every checkpoint. Pony wants its score tags, Illustrious wants different LoRAs, Flux reads plain sentences. WP Model Info looks at the model you loaded and writes what it found into the Context, so the rest of the pipeline can react to it.
$model_family
The architecture, read from the loaded model itself: sd15, sdxl, flux, sd3, chroma and so on. Needs the model input.
$model_variant
The fine-tune line, read from the checkpoint's file name by the variant rules: pony, illustrious, noobai, animagine, or empty when no rule matches.
$model_name
The checkpoint's file name without folders or extension, e.g. ponyDiffusionV6XL.
Pony and Illustrious are both SDXL underneath, so $model_family reads sdxl for both. $model_variant tells them apart, and it can only come from the file name.

sections.title: Where it goes
sections.text:
Figure: Model Info heads the chain, so every Context after it can read the model variables. Steps: Load Checkpoint (MODEL) → model → WP Model Info ($model_variant) → context → WP Context (rules branch on it). Flow diagram of three stages left to right: Load Checkpoint (MODEL), an arrow labelled MODEL, WP Model Info ($model_variant), an arrow labelled context, and WP Context (rules branch on it). Caption: Model Info heads the chain, so every Context after it can read the model variables.
If a node that loads LoRAs from the prompt sits on the model, wire Model Info to the MODEL from before that node. Otherwise the prompt needs the model and the model needs the prompt, and ComfyUI refuses to run the loop.

sections.title: Ports & widget
sections.text:
upstream (in)
An existing Context to extend. Only nodes after Model Info see its variables, so it usually goes first.
model (in)
The MODEL from your checkpoint loader. Gives the family, and the node follows the wire back to the loader for the file name, stepping over LoRA loaders and other model patches.
Detected
The three values and where each comes from. Variant and name update as soon as you change the loader's checkpoint; the family shows after the first run.
Globe
Whether the Assembler can use the variable. All three start internal: later rules read them, but the Assembler leaves them out of the prompt and its variable chips. Click the globe to use one in the Assembler.
Pin
Use your own value for a row instead of the detected one: a file name when no model is wired, or a variant to try your Pony rules without switching checkpoint. Click it again to go back to detection.
Variant rules
Variant + pattern rows. The first pattern found in the file name sets $model_variant and its row lights up. Case-insensitive; | separates alternatives. A broken row is outlined in red and skipped with a WP Debug warning. Reset puts the shipped rules back.
context (out)
The upstream Context plus the three variables. To use a value outside the pipeline, turn its globe off and put it in an Assembler template.

sections.title: LoRAs per model
sections.text: In the derivation editor, LoRA by model adds a ready-made rule: if $model_variant is pony, set $loras to a Pony LoRA tag; if illustrious, an Illustrious one; otherwise leave it empty. Swap the placeholder LoRA names for yours, add branches for other variants, and put $loras in your Assembler template. The same pattern works for quality tags, negatives or anything else a derivation can write.

sections.title: Constraints from the model
sections.text:
Constraints react to a wildcard's pick, not to a variable, so the model reaches them through a wildcard. Make a wildcard (say Model) with options pony and illustrious, tag them, add it to your Context, and in its node settings set Match variable to model_variant. Instead of rolling, it picks the option whose text equals the detected variant, and any constraint can use it as its source, for example “if Model is pony, exclude photo styles”.
Mark one option of that wildcard as the fallback (for example “other”), so checkpoints your rules don't recognise still get a predictable pick. Without a fallback the wildcard rolls as usual and WP Debug notes that nothing matched.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
The canvas previews $model_variant and $model_name from the loader's file name straight away. $model_family needs the loaded model, so it previews as a placeholder until the first run (or pin it).
Model Info changes nothing in your library, so shared modules that branch on $model_variant need no schema update.
