pages.title: WP Prompt Assembler
pages.blurb: Fill $var placeholders in a template string.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
Write a template like a $style portrait of $subject, $lighting and the Assembler substitutes every $variable from the upstream Context. The result is a plain text string you send straight to a CLIP Text Encode or any other text consumer. Variables marked as internal in the Context are kept out of the rendered prompt automatically.
Figure: WP Prompt Assembler with template '$mood, $subject, $style, $accent, masterpiece, highly detailed'. The variables strip below the template lists 3 upstream chips ($style, $scene, $accent) on the left + 2 dashed-orange missing chips ($mood, $subject) on the right, with a hover tooltip 'Click to remove $mood from template · Right-click for more'. Header counters read '3 upstream · 2 missing'. Resolved preview shows the upstream chips filled in ('oil painting', 'cinematic lighting') while the missing slots stay literal as '$mood, $subject' so the gap is obvious. Close-up screenshot of a WP Prompt Assembler. The template reads '$mood, $subject, $style, $accent, masterpiece, highly detailed', and the variables header shows 3 upstream · 2 missing. The chip strip lists $style, $scene and $accent as available chips, then mood and subject as dashed amber missing chips with a warning icon; a tooltip over mood says 'Click to remove $mood from template · Right-click for more'. The resolved preview reads '$mood, $subject, oil painting, cinematic lighting, masterpiece, highly detailed', leaving the missing variables literal so the gap is obvious.

sections.title: Inputs & output
sections.text:
context (in)
The resolved variable map from any WP Context chain. Required — without it the node has no values to substitute.
template
Your prompt template. Type free text and insert $variable names wherever you want a wildcard pick or fixed value to appear. The multiline editor supports the full variable syntax.
negative_template
Optional. The negative template, in the collapsible negative section under the preview. $negatives marks where the collected negative words go; it reads $vars too. Leave it empty to output just the collected words. Like the template, it can be turned into an input and wired from any STRING.
prompt (out)
The fully resolved prompt string. Wire it directly into a CLIP Text Encode, a WP Prompt Cleaner, or any other node that accepts a STRING. Stays output 0, so existing links never move.
negative (out)
The negative words of every variable the template rendered, filled into the negative template. Wire it into your negative CLIP Text Encode (or the Cleaner's negative input).

sections.title: Writing templates
sections.text:
The Assembler's one job is to drop $variable values into your text:
- $varname — replaced with the value from the Context. If no binding exists, the placeholder resolves to empty and the canvas preview highlights it with an amber underline so you can spot the gap before running. The output is tidied after: commas left at the start or end, and a joining word left with nothing after it because its variable came out empty ("shadows with, rain"), are dropped. Words your own text ends on ("shirt tucked in") and emoticon tags (":d", "!?") are kept as written.
- $$ — a literal dollar sign, in case you need one in the output text.
Inline picks like {a|b|c} are not rolled here. The Assembler has no seed of its own, so a pick would freeze on the same branch every run — instead it leaves the {a|b|c} in the prompt verbatim. To get a real random pick, produce the value in a seeded module — a Wildcard, Combine, or Derivation inside a WP Context — and reference its $variable in the template instead.
The Variables strip below the template lists every upstream binding — click any chip to insert $name at the cursor position rather than typing it by hand.

sections.title: The negative output
sections.text:
Options, fixed values, combines and derivations can carry negative words for the variable they set. The negative output collects them, but only for the variables this template actually rendered, so a detailer Assembler that renders just $face never picks up the hair negatives. Internal variables add nothing.
- $negatives in the negative template marks where the collected words go, e.g. lowres, bad anatomy, $negatives.
- An empty negative template outputs just the collected words.
- A negative template without $negatives gets them appended at the end.
- Repeated tags are dropped (case-insensitive, and weight wraps like (blurry:1.2) count as the plain tag), including tags already in the negative template. A $var in the negative template adds its text, not its own negatives.
Keep your standing negative (lowres, bad anatomy) in the negative template and let $negatives add the words this run's picks call for. See Negatives for where negative words come from.

sections.title: Save & Load template
sections.text: The toolbar buttons let you save the current template to the Templates library or load a previously saved one. After loading, the next Save defaults to updating that same library entry. Manage all templates in the SPA Templates tab.

pages.title: WP Prompt Cleaner
pages.blurb: Rule-based cleanup of a prompt string.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
Wire any prompt string — typically from a WP Prompt Assembler — into the Cleaner and it applies a configurable set of rules: whitespace normalization, prompt syntax tidying (empty groups, nested weights, LoRA tags), tag deduplication, fuzzy matching, and an optional blocklist. The cleaned text comes out the other side ready to wire into a CLIP Text Encode. It works on text alone and needs no Context connection.
Figure: WP Prompt Cleaner fed a deliberately messy 40-word / 297-char tag dump (duplicate 'highly detailed', orphan '!!' + '---' punctuation, near-duplicates like 'ultra realistic' vs 'ultra-realistic', blocklist hits watermark / low quality / bad anatomy / signature). Mode = tags · Intensity = aggressive. Rules pane lists hits per family — whitespace 3 · punctuation 6 · tag dedupe 3 · fuzzy dedupe 3 · blocklist 4 — plus a 'Blocklist · 4 entries · list' button. The Show Any node on the right renders the cleaned single-line output. Screenshot of a WP Prompt Cleaner feeding a Show Any node. The input is a messy tag list (40 words, 297 characters) with doubled spaces, stray commas, '!!' and '---', repeats like 'highly detailed' and 'freckles', near-duplicates like 'ultra realistic' and 'ultra-realistic', and tags such as watermark, low quality, bad anatomy and signature. Mode is tags and Intensity is aggressive; the Rules list counts whitespace 3, punctuation 6, tag dedupe 3, fuzzy dedupe 3 and blocklist 4, above a Blocklist button showing 4 entries. Show Any prints the cleaned single line, with the duplicates, junk punctuation and blocklisted tags gone.

sections.title: Inputs & output
sections.text:
prompt (in)
The text to clean. Typically from a WP Prompt Assembler, but works with any STRING source.
cleaner widget
Configure the cleaning rules: pick a mode, set an intensity preset, toggle individual rules on or off, and manage the blocklist. The widget also shows run-stats after each execution.
negative (in)
Optional. A negative prompt to clean alongside the prompt — type it in the box or wire one in, typically the Assembler's negative output. Left empty, the negative output is empty.
prompt (out)
The cleaned text, ready to wire into a CLIP Text Encode or any other text consumer. Stays output 0.
negative (out)
The cleaned negative, using the negative column's rules. Wire it into your negative CLIP Text Encode.

sections.title: Mode
sections.text: Choose Tags mode when your prompt is a comma-separated tag list (the default for most SD workflows). The cleaner splits on commas, applies all rules per-tag, and reassembles. Choose Text mode for prose-style prompts — tag-only rules like deduplication are disabled, and the blocklist removes matched words without pulling the whole phrase.

sections.title: Intensity presets
sections.text:
Gentle
Whitespace normalization only — collapses extra spaces, strips leading/trailing gaps. Safest option when you want minimal changes.
Balanced
Adds empty-group removal, LoRA tag spacing, punctuation cleanup and exact tag deduplication on top of gentle. None of these change what the prompt means. Good default for most prompt workflows.
Aggressive
Also merges nested weights and enables fuzzy deduplication, which catches near-duplicate tags that differ by pluralisation or minor spelling. May occasionally merge things you intended to keep separate.
Custom
No preset — a Custom badge lights up when your per-rule toggles diverge from the active preset level.

sections.title: Prompt syntax rules
sections.text:
Three rules read the prompt the way ComfyUI does. They work in both modes and run first, so the commas and spaces they leave behind are tidied in the same run.
Empty groups
Removes brackets with nothing inside: (), [], ( , ), (:1.2), and groups left empty once those go. red (), dress becomes red, dress. The usual source is a weighted ref that resolved to nothing: (@{hat}:1.2) becomes (:1.2). On from Balanced.
Merge weights
Folds stacked weights into one group by multiplying them, as ComfyUI does (a bare ( ) counts as 1.1): ((a:1.1):1.2) becomes (a:1.32), (((a))) becomes (a:1.33), and (a:1.0) becomes plain a. Only merges when the inner group is everything inside the outer one, rounds to 2 decimals, and never touches [ ]. On in Aggressive.
LoRA spacing
Tidies <lora:…> tags (and lyco, locon, hypernet, <embedding:…>): < lora : x : 0.8 > becomes <lora:x:0.8>, and girl<lora:x:1> becomes girl <lora:x:1>. Spaces inside a file name stay. On from Balanced.
Escaped \( \) stay literal, LoRA and embedding names are never edited, and if the brackets don't balance the bracket rules leave the prompt exactly as written.

sections.title: Cleaning the negative
sections.text:
With a negative wired in, one Cleaner cleans both prompts. The rule list gets a second column of checkboxes for the negative, with its own defaults: the same as the prompt column's, except fuzzy dedupe and the blocklist are off. Near-duplicates in a negative ("bad hands", "bad hand") are usually deliberate, and the blocklist's words are often exactly what belongs in a negative. Presets set both columns; changing a negative checkbox marks the preset as custom.
Drop negative tags also in prompt (off by default) removes a tag from the negative when the prompt asks for it too, since the model can't both draw it and avoid it. Either way, the run stats name the tags the two share.

sections.title: Blocklist
sections.text:
Add words or phrases you always want removed. Two modes:
- List — comma or newline-separated words, matched case-insensitively. In tags mode the entire tag containing the match is removed; in text mode only the matched word is removed and any orphan punctuation cleaned up around it.
- Regex — one pattern per line. Patterns are matched case-insensitively. Invalid patterns are skipped and reported in run-stats.
Hover any rule toggle for an inline explanation. After each run, the stat counters next to each active rule show exactly what was dropped — a quick sanity check that your rules are working as expected.

pages.title: WP Image Filter
pages.blurb: Pause the run and pick which images (and their prompts) go on.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text: Upscaling every image of a batch costs time on the ones you'd throw away. Put WP Image Filter between the first KSampler and the upscaler: the run stops there, a picker shows every image, and only the ones you pick continue. Everything that belongs to an image travels with it, so the upscaler gets each picked image's own latent, conditioning and prompt.

sections.title: Where it goes
sections.text:
Figure: Wire the same conditioning and prompt text through the filter that the upscaler would otherwise take from the start. Steps: KSampler + VAE Decode (images, latent) → images + prompts → WP Image Filter (you pick) → picks → Upscaler (picked only). Flow diagram of three stages left to right: KSampler + VAE Decode (images, latent), an arrow labelled images + prompts, WP Image Filter (you pick), an arrow labelled picks, and Upscaler (picked only). Caption: wire the same conditioning and prompt text through the filter that the upscaler would otherwise take from the start, so only the picked images and their matching data go on.
With a Context Loop, every iteration is a frame. The picker groups images by frame, and the prompt, conditioning and Context of a frame are kept only when one of its images is.

sections.title: Inputs & outputs
sections.text:
Every input has a matching output. Connect only what you need.
images
The images to pick from. Required: this is what the picker shows.
latent, masks
Sliced to the picked images. A mask you paint in the picker replaces that image's mask.
positive, negative
CONDITIONING. A batched conditioning is sliced with the images; a single one is kept for every frame that keeps an image.
positive_text, negative_text
The prompt strings, kept or dropped with their frame.
context
Each frame's WP Context, kept or dropped with it.
clip (in)
Optional. Re-encodes a prompt you edit in the picker, so the positive/negative conditioning follows the edit. Without it, an edit changes only the text outputs.
extra_1, extra_2
Any type. The output takes the type of what you connect. Batched values are sliced, anything else follows its frame.
picks (out)
What was kept, as frame:image (1-based), for example 1:2, 3:1.

sections.title: The picker
sections.text:
Click
Pick or unpick an image. A frame's all button picks the whole frame; Ctrl+A picks everything.
Frame
Click the frame around an image (its border or label) to zoom in, where you can compare, edit the prompt and paint a mask. The Zoom & refine button in the header does the same.
Space
Zoom the image under the mouse, or leave the zoom (same as Zoom & refine). In the zoom, ←/→ move and ↑ picks. The picker remembers: leave it zoomed and the next one opens zoomed.
F
Fit: make the images as big as the picker allows, so a few images fill the screen. Same as the Fit button; remembered for next time.
I
In the zoom: Details. Lists the frame's variable values (Copy copies them) and seed, shows the frame's other images with Pick whole frame, and marks each value in the positive prompt (click it to edit). Remembered for next time.
C
In the zoom: pin this image, then step to another to compare the two with a slider. C again stops.
M
In the zoom: paint a mask on this image (brush, eraser, size, invert, clear).
Enter
Keep the picks and let the run go on.
Escape
Tuck the picker away. A waiting pill at the bottom of the screen opens it again, picks intact.
Keep all sends everything on. Stop branch stops the nodes after this one; the rest of the run finishes normally. Cancelling the run closes the picker.
A short chime plays when the picker opens, and the tab title starts with ● Pick images while something waits, so you notice from another tab. Turn the chime off with Image Filter sound in Settings; turn on Image Filter desktop notification to also get a system notification while the tab is in the background.

sections.title: Labels, sweep grid and Send to Loop
sections.text:
With a Context Loop, each frame is labelled with its number and the options its sweep pinned (for example #3 · red · pencil). Hover a label to see the frame's seed and prompt. A sweep of two or more wildcards opens as a grid. The bar above it picks which wildcard goes on Rows and which on Columns (⇄ swaps them); any others Split by, one small grid per value. Click a row, column or group name to pick all of it. Frames in the header switches back to the list.
Send to Loop writes your picks back to the loop: the picked frames' seeds are locked (when the loop overrides seeds) and every other frame is bypassed, so the next run repeats only what you kept.

sections.title: Refine before it goes on
sections.text:
In the zoom, the Refine panel edits the frame's positive and negative prompt and paints a mask for the upscaler. Edits travel with the picks; tiles show ✎ for an edited prompt and ◐ for a painted mask.
- An edited prompt replaces the text output. Wire a CLIP into the filter's clip input and the conditioning is re-encoded to match; without one the conditioning stays as it was, and the panel says so.
- With Same shape a frame's picks go on together, so a prompt edit covers the whole frame. With One per image it covers just that image.
- A painted mask goes to the masks output, resized to the image. Images you don't paint keep the incoming mask, or an empty one when nothing is wired in.
Figure: How the picks carry over. Diagram titled How the picks carry over: 3 frames of 2 images from a Context Loop; frame 1 image 1 and both frame 2 images are picked, frame 3 none. Rows compare IN with OUT (same shape): images, latent and masks keep only the picked items of frames 1 and 2 (frame 2 gets a PAINTED mask); positive / negative keep 'cond red' and turn 'cond blonde' into 'cond blonde, freckles' marked RE-ENCODED; positive text becomes 'blonde hair, freckles…' marked EDITED. Notes: per-frame items follow their frame, batched ones are sliced; an edited prompt is re-encoded when a CLIP is wired; One per image emits single-image items.

sections.title: Settings on the node
sections.text:
Mode
Pause & pick asks every run. Reuse last picks keeps the same picks without asking, and asks again when they no longer fit. Pass all lets everything through.
Send picks as
Same shape keeps each frame's picks together as one batch. One per image sends every pick as its own item, with its own copy of its frame's prompt, conditioning and Context.
Timeout
Seconds to wait; 0 waits until you answer. After a timeout it keeps all, keeps the first image, or stops the branch.
The Last run strip under the settings shows what the last run kept.

pages.title: WP Debug
pages.blurb: Inspect the Context: snapshot, trace, picks, warnings.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
Drop a WP Debug node anywhere and wire a Context output into it. After each Generate the built-in viewer fills with a tabbed snapshot of everything that flowed through that point. It has no output — it is a read-only observation tool that updates every run so you always see fresh data.
Figure: A WP Context expanding the Starter set bundle (6 modules) into a WP Debug. Debug's Snapshot tab is selected from the four-tab strip (Snapshot / Trace / Picks / Warnings) and the JSON pane lists this run's resolved $vars: subject=tiger, mood=dramatic, style=oil painting, scene=dramatic tiger, accent=cinematic lighting — exactly what every downstream Assembler will see. Screenshot of a WP Context feeding a WP Debug. The Context (seed randomized, modules 6 / 6) has the Starter set bundle expanded: Starter subject, Starter pairing, Starter mood, Starter style, Starter scene and Starter accent. The WP Debug has four tabs, Snapshot, Trace (6), Picks (2) and Warnings, with Snapshot selected, showing JSON of this run's resolved values: subject tiger, mood dramatic, style oil painting, scene dramatic tiger, accent cinematic lighting. It shows that the Snapshot tab lists exactly the variables a downstream Assembler would see.

sections.title: Viewer tabs
sections.text:
Variables
Every $variable and its resolved value at this point in the chain, with the step that set it — the quickest way to check that your wildcards rolled what you expected. A variable's negative words sit under its value in red, naming the module they came from when it isn't the variable's own, and the tab bar counts the variables that carry negatives.
Trace
Every step in run order, grouped by Context node. Open a step to see why it did what it did: a wildcard's odds and the constraints that re-weighted it, which derivation branch fired (an Add to negative action reads “negative: …”), and the negative each write left on its variable.
Warnings
Runtime notices: missing variables referenced in templates, constraints that never fired, invalid bindings, and similar issues. Check here first when something looks off.
Raw
The whole snapshot as JSON, including the negatives table. The download button saves it.
Use the filter box at the top of each tab to search by variable name or warning type when the list is long.

sections.title: Placement tips
sections.text:
Wire the debug node after a specific Context to inspect that stage of the chain, or wire it after the final Context to see the complete resolved map. You can have multiple debug nodes at different points in the same workflow — each shows what it sees at its own position.
Figure: Two debug points on the same workflow. Left pair: WP Context with the Starter set bundle expanded → WP Debug snapshot reads subject=wolf, mood=dramatic, style=oil painting, scene=dramatic wolf, accent=cinematic lighting. Right pair: a downstream WP Context layering the Alt starter set bundle on top (Alt style / scene / accent rows carry green OVERRIDE pills) → its WP Debug snapshot reads the same wolf + dramatic but with style=concept art …, scene=golden hour cargo dirigible, accent=atmospheric haze, plus the alt-bundle's $vehicle + $weather. Same workflow, two snapshots, one per chain stage. Screenshot of a chain WP Context, WP Debug, WP Context, WP Debug. The first Context holds the Starter set bundle and its Debug Snapshot reads subject wolf, mood dramatic, style oil painting, scene dramatic wolf, accent cinematic lighting. The second Context holds the Alt starter set bundle (Alt subject, Alt pairing, Alt weather, and Alt style, Alt scene, Alt accent each marked OVERRIDE), and its Debug Snapshot keeps wolf and dramatic but reads style 'concept art, dramatic composition, painterly', scene golden hour cargo dirigible, accent atmospheric haze, plus vehicle cargo dirigible and weather golden hour. A Debug after each stage shows what that stage changed.

pages.title: WP Var → Int
pages.blurb: Parse an integer out of a $var.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
Sometimes a wildcard pick contains a number — a resolution like 1920x1080, a step count like 30 steps, or just a plain value like 512. WP Var → Int extracts the number and emits it as a proper integer you can wire into any node that expects one. If the variable is missing or contains no recognisable number, it quietly returns the default you set — it never stops the run.
Figure: Two WP Var → Int nodes both reading the same $resolution variable, picker dropdown open showing the upstream Context's available chips ($subject, $mood, $style, $resolution-highlighted, $scene, $accent). The first node uses index 0 — last execute lands on 1344, 'parsed from 1344×768' — wired into Empty Latent Image's width. The second node uses index 1 — last execute lands on 768 — wired into height. Two Show Any nodes print 1344 and 768 to confirm the round-trip. Screenshot of two WP Var → Int nodes, both reading $resolution; the first has its dropdown open listing $subject, $mood, $style, $resolution, $scene and $accent. The first node uses index 0 and its last execute shows 1344, parsed from '1344x768'; the second uses index 1 and shows 768 from the same text. Their value outputs wire into the width and height inputs of an Empty Latent Image, and two Show Any nodes print 1344 and 768. It shows how the index picks which number to take from a value containing several.

sections.title: Controls
sections.text:
context (in)
The upstream Context carrying the $variable you want to read.
var_name
Pick the $variable to parse from the dropdown. The list updates automatically with every variable available in the upstream Context.
index
Which number to extract when the variable contains more than one. 0 gives the first, 1 the second, and so on. Most variables only have one number, so leave this at 0.
default
The value to use when the variable is missing, has no numbers in it, or the index is beyond what was found. The node never errors — it always falls back to this.
value (out)
The extracted integer, ready to wire into any node that accepts INT — image width, step count, batch size, and so on.

sections.title: How the extraction works
sections.text:
The node scans the variable's text value for signed integers and collects them in order. The index control selects which one to return:
- 1920x1080 — index 0 → 1920, index 1 → 1080
- 30 steps — index 0 → 30
- hello — no numbers found → returns default
To extract both width and height from a single $resolution variable, place two WP Var → Int nodes reading the same variable: one with index 0 for width and one with index 1 for height.

pages.title: WP Var → Float
pages.blurb: Parse a float out of a $var.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
When a wildcard pick contains a decimal value — 0.75, cfg 7.5, or even a plain integer like 8 — WP Var → Float extracts it and emits it as a proper float you can wire into any node that expects one. Plain integers match too, so you can use this node wherever you need FLOAT output even if your variable only ever holds whole numbers. Missing variables or ones with no recognisable number quietly return the default.
Figure: WP Var → Float reading $cfg, picker dropdown open over upstream chips ($subject, $mood, $style, $resolution, $cfg-highlighted, $scene, $accent). Index 0, default 0.00, last execute → 7.5 'parsed from 7.5'. The FLOAT output wires into the cfg input on a KSampler (steps 20, sampler_name euler, scheduler simple) sitting alongside it; a Show Any node renders 7.5 to confirm. Screenshot of a WP Var → Float node with its variable dropdown open, listing $subject, $mood, $style, $resolution, $cfg, $scene and $accent, with $cfg selected. The last execute line shows 7.5, parsed from '7.5', with index 0 and default 0.00. Its value output wires into the cfg input of a KSampler (steps 20, sampler_name euler, scheduler simple, denoise 1.00) and into a Show Any that prints 7.5. It shows a variable driving a numeric sampler setting.

sections.title: Controls
sections.text:
context (in)
The upstream Context carrying the $variable you want to read.
var_name
Pick the $variable to parse from the dropdown. The list updates automatically with every variable available in the upstream Context.
index
Which number to extract when the variable contains more than one. 0 gives the first, 1 the second, and so on. Leave at 0 for single-value variables.
default
The value to use when the variable is missing, has no numbers in it, or the index is beyond what was found. The node never errors — it always falls back to this.
value (out)
The extracted float, ready to wire into any node that accepts FLOAT — CFG scale, denoising strength, and similar inputs.

sections.title: How the extraction works
sections.text:
The node scans the variable's text for decimal and scientific-notation numbers. Whole integers match too:
- cfg 7.5 — index 0 → 7.5
- 1920x1080 — index 0 → 1920.0, index 1 → 1080.0
- 1.5e-3 — index 0 → 0.0015
- hello — no numbers found → returns default
Because whole integers match the float pattern, WP Var → Float works as a drop-in when you need a FLOAT output from a variable that holds a whole number.

pages.title: WP Var → Bool
pages.blurb: Parse a boolean out of a $var.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
WP Var → Bool reads a $variable from the upstream Context and interprets its text as a boolean. Words like true, yes, on, and 1 become true; words like false, no, off, and 0 become false. Wire the output into any node that accepts BOOLEAN — a sampler toggle, a switch, a boolean math node — to make that switch probabilistic.
Figure: WP Var → Bool reading $true_or_false, picker dropdown open over upstream chips ($subject, $mood, $style, $resolution, $cfg, $true_or_false-highlighted, $scene, $accent). Index 0, default false. Last execute → True 'parsed from yes' — the parser accepts yes/no/on/off/1/0/true/false. The value output feeds a comfyui-kjnodes BOOL Constant and a Show Any; both Show Any nodes print True. Screenshot of a WP Var → Bool node with its variable dropdown open, listing $subject, $mood, $style, $resolution, $cfg, $true_or_false, $scene and $accent, with $true_or_false selected. The last execute line shows True, parsed from 'yes', and the node has index 0 and default false. Its value output feeds a BOOL Constant (comfyui-kjnodes) and a Show Any, and both Show Any nodes print True. It shows a text variable such as yes being read as a boolean for another node's input.

sections.title: Controls
sections.text:
context (in)
The upstream Context carrying the $variable you want to read.
var_name
Pick the $variable to parse from the dropdown. The list updates automatically with every variable available in the upstream Context.
index
Which boolean token to use when the variable contains more than one recognised value. 0 gives the first match, 1 the second. Words like "maybe" or numbers like 1.5 are ignored and do not count toward the index.
default
The value to use when the variable is missing or contains no recognised boolean words. The node never errors — it always falls back to this.
value (out)
The parsed boolean, ready to wire into any node that accepts BOOLEAN — sampler toggles, switch nodes, and so on.

sections.title: How the parsing works
sections.text:
The node splits the variable's value on spaces, commas, semicolons, pipes, and slashes, then checks each piece against the recognised word lists (case-insensitive). Words that match neither list are skipped entirely — they do not advance the index:
- Truthy words: true, yes, on, 1
- Falsy words: false, no, off, 0
- Everything else (e.g. maybe, 1.5, hello) is ignored
So a variable value of true maybe false has two boolean tokens: index 0 → true, index 1 → false.
Add a wildcard with options on / off and wire it through WP Var → Bool to randomly enable or disable any boolean input in your workflow.

pages.title: Wildcard
pages.blurb: Weighted random pick that sets one $var.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
A Wildcard module holds a list of options — "a cat", "a dog", "a fox" — and picks one (or several) each run. The result is written to a $variable you name, so later modules (and your prompt template) can use it. Options can carry weights so some are more likely than others, you can tag them with several sub-category labels to filter on the fly, and an option's text can even embed another wildcard — see Multi-pick and Nested references below.
Figure: The Starter subject wildcard modal open on the $subject variable. Two sub-category chips (feline · 2, canine · 2) sit above a four-row pool: cat + tiger tagged FELINE, dog + wolf tagged CANINE, each row showing a 25% probability bar and a weight of 1. Footer carries the Lock pick + Hide from prompt runtime toggles plus the Save to library / Save split. Screenshot of the Starter subject Wildcard editor (Library entry, weighted options resolved per pick) with Variable binding $subject. The Pool section (what RNG can pick from) shows two sub-category chips, feline 2 and canine 2, above a table of four enabled options: cat and tiger in category FELINE, dog and wolf in category CANINE, each with weight 1 and a 25% probability bar, summarized as 4 of 4 enabled. Below are the Runtime toggles Lock pick and Hide from prompt and the footer buttons Edit library entry in SPA, Reset overrides, Save to library, Cancel and Save. It shows how weights turn into pick probabilities and how options are grouped into sub-categories.

sections.title: Option fields
sections.text:
Value
The text that goes into the prompt when this option is picked — for example, "a cat", "a dog", or "a fox".
Weight
How likely this option is to be chosen relative to the others. A weight of 2 is twice as likely as a weight of 1. Set to 0 to disable without deleting — and if every option ends up at 0, whether you set them or a constraint excluded them, the wildcard resolves to nothing (or to its fallback, below) rather than quietly using the first one.
Sub-categories
Zero or more labels on an option (e.g. "feline", "warm") — an option can carry several at once. They group options in the editor, form the Constraint matrix axes, power bulk selection, and back the per-use category filter below. Tags can be organised into axes (e.g. species, temperature) so the editor shows grouped pills.
Null option
Marks this option as the "no pick" result — the wildcard resolves to an empty string. At most one option per wildcard can be a null option.
Fallback
Hover an option's probability and click "set as fallback". The fallback rolls like any other option, with its own weight, and is also used when nothing is left to pick: constraints (an Only rule included) excluded every option, the fallback included, or every weight is 0. Give it weight 0 if it should only ever stand in. Without one the wildcard resolves to nothing in that case. One per wildcard; the null option can't be the fallback. Turning the fallback off for one use (its checkbox on the node) keeps the empty result there. WP Debug and the Test Runner say "Fallback used" when it kicks in. Shared wildcards with a fallback are stamped schema 9.

sections.title: Per-use options
sections.text:
When you add a wildcard to a Context you can change how it behaves for that use without touching the shared library entry:
Random mode
Pick any option from the pool using its weights. This is the default.
Subcategory mode
A quick pre-filter that narrows the pool to options carrying a chosen sub-category before the pick. The pick itself is identical to random — only which options are eligible changes. The category filter below is the general, boolean form of it.
Pinned mode
Locks to one specific option regardless of seed. Use this to hold an element steady across a batch while everything else varies.
Category filter
A boolean sub-category expression — "and / or / not", parentheses, and comma as shorthand for "or" (e.g. "feline and warm, not lynx") — that narrows the pool to matching options before the pick. Build it from grouped pills or type it in the advanced editor; it never applies to the null option.
Exclude null
Drops the null option for this use, so the wildcard always resolves to real text. Only shown when the wildcard actually has a null option to exclude.
Match variable
Under Runtime in the node settings. Instead of rolling, pick the option whose text equals a variable's value (ignoring case), e.g. model_variant from WP Model Info. No match uses the fallback option; without one the wildcard rolls as usual and WP Debug notes it. This is how a variable drives a constraint: the matched pick is a normal source pick.
Locked seed
Freezes this wildcard's pick across every loop iteration — every iteration in the batch gets the same result. Useful for holding one element constant (e.g. the art style) while letting other wildcards vary.
Subcategory mode and random mode produce the same result when no sub-category filter is active — subcategory mode is just a convenient way to pre-narrow the pool.

sections.title: Multi-pick
sections.text:
By default a wildcard makes a single pick, but a use can draw several at once. Set the Pick count to a range — a low and a high (make them equal for a fixed count, e.g. 2–2) — and the wildcard rolls that many options. A separator joins them, and Allow repeats decides whether a draw can land on the same option twice: off (the default) keeps the picks distinct, on draws with replacement so repeats are possible.
A multi-pick produces a list value. Reference the joined list with a bare $name (it uses the separator), or pull out a single item with $name.K — K is 0-based, so $colors.0 is the first pick. For example, a $colors wildcard set to Pick 2–3 with separator , might resolve to "red, blue, green", while $colors.0 is just "red".
In multi-pick the null option leaves the pool — set the minimum to 0 when you want "maybe nothing" (a use that sometimes picks fewer, or none). The text-field equivalent of multi-pick is the inline pick syntax, covered on The $variable pipeline.

sections.title: Nested references
sections.text:
An option's value isn't limited to plain text — it can embed a reference to another wildcard with @{uuid}, so picking that option pulls in a fresh pick from the referenced "nested" wildcard. The reference can narrow what the nested wildcard may roll with a :filter sub-category expression and drop its null option with !null — for example @{abcd1234:warm} rolls the nested wildcard but only from its warm-tagged options. Inline {a|b} picks work in option text too. Type @ to insert one; the chip states, the full filter grammar (not / and / or / parentheses) and why plain @name stays text are on Chips & references.
A wildcard is a producer: on its option text, @{} references and {a|b} picks resolve, but $name reads do not — an option can't pull in a value another module set, no matter the order. To build a value from earlier picks, use a Combine or Derivation. The full token grammar and the per-surface gate live on The $variable pipeline.

sections.title: What a tag is, and the two kinds
sections.text:
A sub-category is a label on an option. It filters the pool and drives the Constraint matrix. It is not a variable, and until you say otherwise nothing outside those two places can read it.
Every tag group carries a kind, chosen on the group's header:
classify (default)
The tags describe what the option IS — casual, t-shirt, skirt. Several are true at once, so a constraint on this group uses all of them together (AND). This is how every group has always behaved; leaving it alone changes nothing.
accepts
The tags are alternatives the option OFFERS — an outfit that works with sneakers, heels or sandals. Exactly one is rolled at pick time and read as $var.AXIS, and it's that single rolled tag a constraint keys on — so a diagonal “same tag wins” constraint pins the target to exactly the shoe that was rolled, not the whole accepted set.
The test is what the tag says about the option. "Is this outfit casual?" is classify. "Which shoes go with this outfit?" is accepts.
An accepts group can be read as a variable. If a $outfit wildcard has an accepts group named SHOES, then $outfit.SHOES is the tag rolled for this run — the same value in every template, every module and every chained node, because it is rolled once when the option is picked rather than each time it is read. When the wildcard picks more than one option, $outfit.0.SHOES is the first pick's.
Only accepts groups are readable. Ungrouped tags, and tags in a classify group, stay editor-only — $outfit.SHOES renders as nothing if SHOES was never promoted, and the conflict scanner flags it. An accepts group's name is read as $var.NAME, so it must be letters, digits and underscores starting with a letter; renaming one can strand a template that reads it.

sections.title: Constraint interaction
sections.text:
A Constraint module placed between a source wildcard and this one can tilt the option weights — for example, making "stormy" more likely when the subject was "ocean". The constraint must sit after the source wildcard and before this wildcard in the stack. See the Constraint page for the full picture.
Constraints read picks, not variables. To steer one from a variable (the loaded checkpoint, an injected value), give the source wildcard options that spell the variable's values and set Match variable on it. See WP Model Info for a worked example.
Figure: A WP Context node showing the canonical source → constraint → target stack: Starter subject ($subject · 4 options), Starter pairing (#1 $subject → $mood · 2×2 matrix), Starter mood ($mood · 4 options). The pink left-border on the constraint + target row visually pairs them; the constraint claims the first instance of $mood downstream of itself. Screenshot of a WP Context node (modules 3 / 3) with three expanded rows stacked top to bottom: Starter subject ('$subject · 4 options'), Starter pairing marked #1 ('$subject → $mood · 2×2'), and Starter mood marked #1 ('$mood · 4 options'). The constraint and its target share the #1 marker, and the pink left border on the constraint links it to the stack. It shows the required order: source wildcard first, then the constraint, then the target wildcard it reweights below it.

sections.title: Importing wildcard packs
sections.text:
Coming from A1111 or Forge? Open Import / Export → Wildcard packs and choose a folder, files or a .zip, or drop them on the page. It reads Dynamic Prompts, Prompt Post-Processor (PPP) and Impact Pack wildcards: .txt lists, .yaml / .yml and .json files, and .zip packs of them. Dropping a pack on the Import tab opens it here too.
You go through three steps: load the pack, review the plan, then pick what to import with the usual import picker (everything starts selected).
Lists and their names
Each list is named by its path the way __name__ finds it: animals/cats.txt is animals/cats, and a YAML key clothing: { tops: [...] } is clothing/tops. A list that isn't merged becomes its own wildcard, and its variable is the last part ($cats, $tops).
Merging related lists
With Merge related lists ticked (the default), a folder of small lists becomes one wildcard, like one you'd build by hand: hair/colors/red.txt, hair/colors/blonde.txt and hair/colors/dark.txt become one hair/colors wildcard whose options are tagged red, blonde and dark. Each folder level is a tag group, and lists with the same name in sibling folders share a tag: female/footwear and male/footwear give a gender group (female, male) and a footwear tag, like the axes of a hand-built wildcard. A folder merges when it holds at least two lists and up to 1,000 options over at most three levels; a bigger folder is split into its subfolders. Entry points stay separate, and so does a list that points at another list in the same folder, because a wildcard can't reference itself.
Keep separate
Merged rows show a lists chip. Open one to see each list with its tag and the tag groups, and click Keep these lists separate to import that folder as one wildcard per list again; Merge again under the settings undoes it. Untick Merge related lists to keep every list separate.
Roles
The review sorts every wildcard by what it does in the pack. Entry points build a prompt from other wildcards and nothing else uses them: these are what you drop on a Context. Compositions build on other wildcards and are used by one. Vocabulary is a plain list. Groups are made for globs and folder references.
Carries over
Each wildcard is marked Exact, Close (same outputs, but a setting or label didn't carry over) or Needs a look (some text no longer renders as it did, like a dropped if-condition). Open a row to see why.
Domains
The top folders (or YAML top keys) of the pack. Pick one to review it on its own. Each wildcard goes in a category named after its domain, unless you type one category for all.
Library tag
Every module gets the library tag, which starts as the pack's name, so the whole pack sits together on the Tags page.
Bundles
With Bundle the entry points ticked (the default) the entry points go into one bundle per domain, inside one pack bundle. Lists stay in the library, where the entry points reach them through references, so dropping a bundle rolls the prompts the pack was written to make, not every list. A pack of plain lists gets no bundles.
References
__other__ references become @{} chips that point at the imported wildcard. A reference to a list that was merged points at the merged wildcard, filtered by that list's tags (female and footwear), so it still draws from that list only. A glob like __animals/*__, or a parent key like __clothing__ in Impact packs, becomes a group wildcard that picks one of the matching wildcards, weighted by how many options each has. PPP filters such as __colors'warm'__ become a category filter on the chip.
Choice syntax
{a|b}, weights like {2::a|b} and multi-pick like {2$$a|b|c} keep working, and so does __2$$name__: it picks two different values of name. Open ranges like {-2$$a|b} get their missing end filled in, samplers like {~a|b} pick at random, and the default separator is a comma.
Weights, labels and fallbacks
Weighted lines (3::text), PPP labels ('summer, casual'::text) and PPP's else choice carry over as option weights, sub-categories and the wildcard's fallback. A line written twice becomes one option with twice the weight, so the odds stay the same.
Comments and encoding
Lines starting with # are skipped and kept as the module's description, as is the # text inside multi-line YAML prompts. Text after a # with a space before it is cut (so C# survives). Files saved as UTF-8 or Windows-1252 both read correctly.
Figure: Billions of Wildcards in review: 2,653 lists become 935 wildcards, 1,896 of them merged into 190 tagged wildcards. Open here is clothings/regular, 12 lists merged into one wildcard with a gender tag group (female, male, unisex) and a garment group; each list shows the tags that pick it, and Keep these lists separate undoes the merge. Screenshot of the wildcard import review page for a pack named Billions of Wildcards: 935 wildcards plus 43 groups from 1 file, where 1,896 lists were merged into 190 tagged wildcards. Tiles count 137 Entry point, 386 Composition, 412 Vocabulary and 43 Group, and a How it carries over bar reads Exact 976, Close 0, Needs a look 2. In the middle the search clothings/regular shows one merged wildcard (12 lists, Vocabulary, 782 options) expanded to its source lists such as female + footwear, with a Keep these lists separate button. On the right are Import settings including Merge related lists, and a Continue to import button.
Importing the same pack again finds the wildcards you already have instead of adding copies.
What doesn't carry over. Rows marked Needs a look list what changed. PPP if conditions are removed (the choice stays). Dynamic Prompts variables like ${name} stay as plain text, because a wildcard can't read a variable: rebuild that part with a Combine, which can. Template arguments like __name(var=value)__ are dropped, and a reference to a wildcard the pack doesn't contain stays as plain text.

pages.title: Fixed Values
pages.blurb: Assign explicit name = value bindings.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
A Fixed Values module lets you write plain name = value pairs into the Context. Every time the pipeline runs, those $variables are set to whatever text you typed. Nothing is picked at random (unless you use inline {a|b|c} syntax inside the value), and nothing depends on other modules — it just stamps the values in.
Use it for anything that should stay constant: an artist style like "oil painting", a quality booster like "8k, masterpiece", or a reusable negative-prompt fragment. Drop it at the top of your stack and every module below can read those variables.
Figure: The Starter style Fixed Values modal — two name → value rows ($style = oil painting, $quality = 8k, masterpiece) each with their own enable checkbox, footer reading '2 of 2 enabled · 1 added' to flag the instance-added row over the library baseline. Lock seed + Hide from prompt runtime toggles below. Behind the modal: a WP Context stack with Starter style (MOD-flagged orange border), Starter scene, Starter accent. Screenshot of the Starter style Fixed Values editor (Library entry, static $var → value pairs) open over a WP Context. The Values table has two enabled rows: $style = oil painting, and $quality = 8k, masterpiece, the second highlighted in green as an instance-only addition with a remove button. Under the table are an Add new $var for this instance link and a summary reading '2 of 2 enabled · 1 added'. Below are the Runtime toggles Lock seed and Hide from prompt and the usual footer buttons; behind it the Context lists Starter style (marked MOD), Starter scene and Starter accent. It shows fixed values and how a canvas instance can add a value without changing the library entry.

sections.title: Row fields
sections.text:
Name
The $variable name to set — for example, "style" sets $style.
Value
The text to assign. You can use inline {a|b|c} pick syntax here to add a touch of randomness, but you cannot read other $variables — use Combine for that.
Enable / disable
Turn a row off without deleting it. Useful for toggling optional extras like a quality booster or a negative-prompt fragment.

sections.title: Per-use options
sections.text:
When you add a Fixed Values module to a Context you can adjust it for that use:
Value override
Replace the value of any row for this particular use, without changing the shared library entry. Good for adapting a reusable Fixed Values module to a specific workflow.
Locked seed
Freezes any inline {a|b|c} picks across loop iterations so the value stays the same throughout a batch.
Fixed Values cannot read $variables that other modules have set — it is a producer, not a consumer. If you need to build a value from earlier picks, use a Combine module instead.

pages.title: Combine
pages.blurb: Template-fill $vars into one output $var.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
A Combine module takes a template string you write — like $style portrait of $subject, $mood lighting — and fills in the $variable placeholders with whatever was picked or set earlier in the stack. The filled-in result is written to a single output variable (e.g. $prompt_fragment) that your prompt assembler or further modules can use.
You can also sprinkle {a|b|c} inline picks directly inside the template for any on-the-fly variation that doesn't need its own wildcard.

Preview replays the template verbatim; Resolved swaps in static picks → 'oil painting portrait of cat, serene lighting'. Footer carries Lock seed + Hide from prompt runtime toggles. sections.title: What you type in the template
sections.text:
- $variablename — substituted with whatever that variable holds at this point in the stack. The variable must have been set by an earlier module.
- {a|b|c} — picks one of the options at random inline. Good for small variations you don't need a full wildcard for.
- $$ — a literal $ character in the output (escape if you need to write a dollar sign that shouldn't be treated as a variable).
The manager shows you which $variables your template reads as chips below the template field. If a chip is highlighted as missing, add an upstream module that sets that variable.

sections.title: Per-use options
sections.text:
Template override
Replace the entire template for this particular use without changing the shared library entry.
Output variable
Change which $variable name this combine writes to for this use.

pages.title: Derivation
pages.blurb: IF/ELIF/ELSE rules that mutate the Context.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
A Derivation module runs a set of IF/ELIF/ELSE rules after earlier modules have made their picks. Each rule checks a $variable already in the Context and, if the condition matches, changes one or more variables — replacing, appending to, or prepending to their current values.
For example: IF $subject equals "ocean" → append ", with crashing waves" to $mood. If not, the rule does nothing and the next rule is checked.
Figure: The Starter accent Derivation modal — a single Rule 1 condition reading '$mood = dramatic → $accent = cinematic lighting' (the engine falls through to the rule's else branch when $mood resolves to anything else). Footer carries Lock seed + Hide from prompt toggles. Behind the modal: a WP Context with Starter scene + Starter accent stacked, the accent row's orange left-border matching the derivation kind colour. Screenshot of the Starter accent Derivation editor (Library entry, conditional rule-based variable rewrites) open over a WP Context. Under Rules there is one enabled row, Rule 1, reading '$mood = dramatic → $accent = cinematic lighting'. Below are the Runtime toggles Lock seed and Hide from prompt and the footer buttons Edit library entry in SPA, Reset overrides, Save to library, Cancel and Save. Behind the editor the Context shows the Starter scene row (marked MOD) above the Starter accent row. It demonstrates a rule that sets one variable based on the value of another.

sections.title: How rules work
sections.text:
Each Derivation module can hold multiple rules. Every rule is checked from top to bottom — even if an earlier rule fired, the next one is still evaluated independently. Within a single rule, only the first matching branch (IF, ELIF, or ELSE) runs.
Because rules are independent, you can chain several simple rules instead of writing one very complex one. It also means two rules can both fire in the same run if their conditions are both true.

sections.title: Condition operators
sections.text:
equals / not equals
Matches when the variable's value is (or isn't) exactly the text you provide. Case-sensitive.
contains / does not contain
Matches when the variable's value includes the text you provide somewhere inside it (or doesn't).
matches / does not match
Matches using a regular expression — for flexible pattern-based conditions. A broken pattern never matches either way.
NOT
The NOT switch next to a test turns it around: is → is not, contains → does not contain, matches → does not match, exists → does not exist. Does not contain and does not match need schema 10, so a pack using them installs only on this version or newer.
exists / not exists
Matches when the variable is present in the Context (or absent), regardless of its value. Under exists, a switch narrows it: any, is empty (present but empty, e.g. a wildcard that rolled its null option) or has value. Under NOT exists there is nothing to narrow, so the switch is hidden. An older test stored as is unset (missing or empty) still shows the switch on has value, so it keeps its meaning until you pick any.
is set / is unset
is set matches when the variable is present and non-empty; is unset matches when it's absent or empty.

sections.title: Combining tests with AND / OR
sections.text:
A branch can check more than one thing. Click + Condition under a test to add another; the connector between them reads AND (every test must match) and one click flips it to OR (any test may match).
Each connector flips on its own, and AND binds tighter than OR, the way it reads. Turn the second connector of "a AND b AND c" to OR and you get (a AND b) OR c: the tests still joined by AND are drawn as a boxed group, so the page always shows what runs. Flip it back and the box goes away.
You can also build the box yourself with + Group. A group is a boxed list of its own with the opposite connector, so IF $time equals "night" AND ($weather equals "rain" OR $weather equals "fog") is one test plus a group of two. + Group nests up to three levels deep.
Removing tests until one is left turns the branch back into a plain single test, so a derivation only needs the newer format when it really combines tests. An older Wildcard Pipeline refuses a shared pack that does and asks for an update.

sections.title: Action modes
sections.text:
Replace
Overwrite the variable's current value entirely with the action text.
Append
Add the action text to the end of the variable's current value.
Prepend
Insert the action text before the variable's current value.
Add to negative
Leave the variable's text alone and add the action text to its negative words, so they follow the variable into any Assembler that renders it. The value takes $vars, @{refs} and {a|b}; refs resolve quietly and never change a pick.
Replace negative
Like Add to negative, but the action text becomes the variable's only negative words: whatever it carried before is dropped. The variable's own text is still left alone.
Negatives travel with the value. Replace swaps the variable's negatives for those of the variables its new text read; Append and Prepend keep the old ones and add. For example, IF $mood equals "gloomy" → Add to negative "bright colors, smiling" keeps smiles out of every image that renders $mood. A derivation that uses Add to negative is shared as schema 8, which older versions refuse with a request to update.

sections.title: Several actions in one branch
sections.text:
Click + And under a branch's action to add another. The actions run in order when the branch fires, and each one sees what the one before it wrote. For example, IF $tier equals "warmup" THEN $pose Replace $pose_portrait AND $pose Add to negative $pose_portrait.neg. The ELSE branch works the same way. On the canvas, each action gets its own value override.
A branch with more than one action is shared as schema 8, which older versions refuse with a request to update.

sections.title: Nested references in actions
sections.text:
An action's value isn't limited to plain text. When a rule fires, its action value is fully resolved before it's written — so it can embed a @{uuid} reference to another wildcard, an inline {a|b} pick, and $variable reads, all in the same string. A reference can carry the same segments as anywhere else: a :filter sub-category expression to narrow the nested wildcard's pool and !null to drop its null option.
For example, an action $accent = cinematic lighting, @{abcd1234:dramatic} writes "cinematic lighting," followed by a fresh pick from the nested @{abcd1234} wildcard, drawn only from its dramatic-tagged options. This lets a rule conditionally pull in a whole nested wildcard's result rather than a fixed phrase.
Actions and conditions are not symmetric. An action value resolves @{} refs and {a|b} picks; a condition value — the text you compare against — does not. A condition is a plain literal or a $variable, so @{} and {a|b} stay verbatim there and won't match what you expect. This mirrors the per-surface gate on The $variable pipeline.

sections.title: Reading multi-pick variables
sections.text: A rule can read a multi-pick result the same way templates do. Reference the joined list with a bare $colors (it uses the variable's separator), or pull out a single item with $colors.0 — K in $name.K is 0-based, so $colors.0 is the first pick. This works in both condition and action values. The full grammar lives on The $variable pipeline.

sections.title: LoRA by model
sections.text: The LoRA by model button in the editor adds a ready-made rule for use with the WP Model Info node: if $model_variant is pony it sets $loras to a Pony LoRA tag, if illustrious to an Illustrious one, and otherwise to nothing. Replace the placeholder LoRA names with yours, add a branch per variant you use, and put $loras in your Assembler template.

sections.title: Per-use options
sections.text:
When you add a Derivation to a Context you can tune which rules are active for that use:
Disable a rule
Skip one of the top-level IF/ELIF/ELSE rules for this use without removing it from the library entry.
Disable a branch
Skip a specific IF, ELIF, or ELSE branch within a rule for this use.
Value override
Replace the text that a specific branch action writes, or the value a condition compares against, for this use only. A branch that combines tests gets one condition field per test.
Rule order
Reorder the rules for this use without changing the shared library entry.

pages.title: Constraint
pages.blurb: Reweight a target wildcard from a source pick.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
A Constraint module watches the pick made by a source wildcard and then adjusts the option weights of a target wildcard further down the stack — before that target makes its own pick. The constraint itself sets no $variables and produces no text; its entire effect is the nudge it gives to the target.
For example: source wildcard $weather picked "stormy" → boost "dramatic" and "moody" in $mood, reduce "sunny" and "cheerful". The target still picks randomly — you're just shifting the odds.
Figure: The Starter pairing constraint modal — source Starter subject (feline/canine sub-categories) → target Starter mood (calm/intense). The 2×2 rule matrix boosts feline×intense + canine×calm by ×3.0 and reduces the mismatched diagonals to ×0.3. One Exceptions row below overrides tiger → sleepy to EXCLUDE so the EXTRA-tagged exception wins over the matrix boost when both apply. Screenshot of the Starter pairing Constraint editor on the canvas (Library entry, source pick modifies target option weights). Under Rule matrix, the source is Starter subject and the target is Starter mood; the grid crosses feline and canine (rows) with calm and intense (columns): feline × calm ×0.3, feline × intense ×3.0, canine × calm ×3.0, canine × intense ×0.3, with a Legend button beneath. The Exceptions section holds one row tagged EXTRA, tiger → sleepy, set to EXCLUDE, plus an Add extra exception button. It shows sub-category rules adjusting the odds broadly, while an exception overrides one specific value pair.

sections.title: The flow
sections.text: Figure: The constraint nudges the odds of its downstream target instances — every match by default, or a narrower set you choose. It sets no $vars itself. Steps: Source wildcard (its pick) → if it lands on x → Constraint (reweights) → limits → Target wildcard (picks to match). Flow diagram of three stages left to right: Source wildcard (its pick), an arrow labelled if it lands on X, Constraint (reweights), an arrow labelled limits, and Target wildcard (picks to match). Caption: the constraint nudges the odds of its downstream target instances, every match by default or a narrower set you choose, and it sets no $vars itself.

sections.title: Reweight modes
sections.text:
Allow
No change (shown as Neutral in the matrix). The pair rolls as if there were no rule.
Exclude
These options are removed from the pool; everything else remains.
Boost
These options have their weight increased, making them more likely without removing anything.
Reduce
These options have their weight decreased, making them less likely without removing anything.
Only
Links picks: only these options can be picked, and every option without a rule of its own in the same row is removed. Extensions from before this rule existed refuse community packs that use it and ask you to update.
Exception rules (per-option pairs) win over sub-category matrix rules when both apply to the same option. Use exceptions for precise overrides and the matrix for broad category nudges.

sections.title: Stack order matters
sections.text:
The Constraint module must sit after its source wildcard and before its target wildcard in the stack. The engine runs modules top-to-bottom, so position controls the source → constraint → target chain.
By default a Constraint re-weights every matching target instance below it. Use the Target reach selector (below) to narrow that to the first, the next N, or a hand-picked set — and remember that position in the stack decides which instances are even reachable, since a constraint only sees targets after it.

sections.title: Target reach
sections.text:
By default a constraint re-weights every matching target instance it can reach downstream. The per-instance Target reach selector narrows that scope:
All
Default — re-weight every matching target instance downstream of the constraint.
First
Only the first target instance after the constraint; later ones roll unconstrained.
Next N
The next N target instances (you set the count); the rest roll unconstrained.
Pick
Only specific target rows you tick — direct instances, or nested-ref carrier options that reach the target.
If a constraint's reach lands on zero reachable targets — e.g. its only target sits above it, or you picked rows that aren't downstream — the editor flags it constraint_orphan_target so the dead pairing doesn't fail silently.
A constraint can also rule out every option of its target for some source value (each one excluded, shut out by an Only rule, or weighted 0). If the target has no fallback it would come out empty, so the constraint row gets a rules out all badge before you run; hover it to see which source values do it. Allow an option for those values, or mark one of the target's options as its fallback.

sections.title: Preview
sections.text: The Preview card under the exceptions shows what the constraint does in numbers: one row per source option, one column per target option, and in each cell the chance that target option is picked when the source picked that row. It counts the target's own weights, the matrix and the exceptions. A dash means the option is ruled out; a row marked nothing left would leave the target empty, and fallback means the target's fallback option stands in. Other constraints, filters and toggles are left out.

sections.title: Reattach a broken axis
sections.text:
A constraint points at two wildcards by id — its source and its target. If one of those isn't in your library (you installed the constraint without its wildcards, or deleted one later), that axis is stranded: the editor shows the dead id with its remembered name and locks the rule matrix read-only until you fix it.
Use Reattach to re-point the stranded axis at a local wildcard — or Download from community to pull the missing one. The matrix and exceptions then remap onto the new wildcard's sub-categories; any rows that don't exist there are dropped (the editor previews the count before you confirm).

sections.title: Deeper topics
sections.text: Full constraint mechanics — matrix vs exception priority, how constraints carry through nested references, the Target reach selectors in detail, and the "never fired" runtime notice — are covered on the Constraints concept page.

pages.title: Bundles
pages.blurb: Group a range of modules into a reusable unit.

sections.title: What bundles are
sections.text:
A Bundle is a named container that holds several modules together — not a module kind itself. Think of it as a saved preset: you author a combination of wildcards, fixed values, derivations, or whatever you like, save them as a bundle, and then drop that bundle into any Context widget without having to recreate the same setup each time.
At runtime, bundle children run as if they were placed directly in the stack — the bundle is just a grouping layer for the editor.
Figure: A WP Context with two expanded bundles side by side. 'Starter set' (orange MODIFIED chip · 7 mods) wraps Starter subject + pairing + mood. 'Alt starter set' (blue frame, ‌drop-target highlighted) holds Alt subject + pairing + weather + style + scene + accent. Below the bundles, three loose DUPLICATE-flagged rows (Starter style / scene / accent) show how the canvas warns when modules already live inside a bundle above. Screenshot of one WP Context node (seed randomized, modules 12 / 12) holding nested bundles. The Starter set bundle, marked MODIFIED, is expanded and contains Starter subject, Starter pairing and Starter mood, then a nested Alt starter set bundle, highlighted in blue, containing Alt subject, Alt pairing, Alt weather, Alt style, Alt scene and Alt accent. Below the nested bundle are three rows, Starter style, Starter scene and Starter accent, each outlined in amber with a DUPLICATE badge. It shows how bundles nest inside one Context and how the canvas flags modules that appear more than once in the stack.

sections.title: Frozen snapshots
sections.text:
When you insert a bundle into a Context, the editor takes a snapshot of its children at that moment. If you later edit the bundle's library entry, those changes do not flow into existing snapshots — each use is independent.
This is intentional: a bundle is a point-in-time capture of a known-working setup. If the original bundle is later deleted from the library, the snapshot keeps working and the row simply shows a MISSING badge to let you know it is no longer linked to a live library entry.
To pick up changes from the library entry, use "Push to library" from the bundle's context menu to sync the snapshot back up, or re-insert a fresh copy.

sections.title: Disabling a bundle
sections.text: Each bundle has its own enable/disable toggle. Turning a bundle off suppresses all of its children without changing their individual settings. Turn it back on and everything restores exactly as it was — nothing is lost.

sections.title: Bundles and the wildcard cascade
sections.text: When you delete a wildcard from the library, the manager offers to clean up every use of that wildcard across your Contexts. Bundles are intentionally excluded from this cascade — their children are frozen snapshots, so they continue to work correctly even after the source wildcard is gone.

pages.title: Templates
pages.blurb: Save a reusable $var prompt string for the Assembler.

sections.title: What a template is
sections.text:
A prompt template is just the text you feed the WP Prompt Assembler: a mix of literal words and $variable placeholders like $scene, $style, $accent, masterpiece, highly detailed. At runtime the Assembler swaps each $var for whatever your modules produced and emits the finished prompt.
Templates aren't a module kind and they don't sit in a Context stack — they're saved Assembler strings you can name, reuse across workflows, and edit in one place. Think of them as the prompt-shaped counterpart to a bundle: a bundle reuses a set of modules, a template reuses the wording that stitches their $variables together.

sections.title: How it pairs with the Assembler
sections.text:
In a workflow, the WP Prompt Assembler node holds the template string. Saving that string to your library makes a Template; loading a Template back into the Assembler drops the whole string in at once. The Assembler's toolbar has Save and Load buttons wired directly to this library.
Any $var in the template must be produced by a module upstream of the Assembler. If a placeholder has no matching variable at runtime it resolves to empty (the assembler preview underlines it) so you can spot the gap — add a module (or fix the name) that sets it.

pages.title: Warning & conflict types
pages.blurb: Every runtime warning + scanner rule, explained.

sections.title: As you build (canvas)
sections.text:
The scanner watches your graph and flags these straight away:
What it flags | Severity | What it means
Shadowed variable | info | An upstream Context already sets this variable; this one overrides it (last write wins). Normal when chaining — shown so the override is visible.
Duplicate variable | warn | Two modules in the same Context set the same variable name; the lower one wins.
Missing variable in template | warn | The Prompt Assembler template references a $variable that no upstream module produces.
Constraint source not found | warn | A constraint points at a source wildcard that isn't in your library.
Constraint target not found | warn | A constraint points at a target wildcard that isn't in your library.
Constraint source not upstream | warn | The constraint's source wildcard doesn't appear before the constraint in the chain, so it can't read a pick from it.
Constraint target not downstream | warn | No copy of the target wildcard appears after the constraint. Each constraint needs its own downstream target — N constraints on the same wildcard need N copies.
Rules out all (no fallback) | warn | For some value of the constraint's source, every option of the target ends up excluded or weighted 0, and the target has no fallback, so it would come out empty. The hover message lists those source values. Allow at least one option for them, or set a fallback on the target wildcard.
Injector binding unmatched | warn | A WP Context Injector row names a variable that nothing upstream produces.
Unknown tag axis | warn | A $var.AXIS read names an accepts axis the wildcard doesn't declare, so it resolves to empty. Promote that tag group to accepts, or fix the axis name in the read.
Option misses its accepts-axis tag | info | Some options of an accepts-axis wildcard carry none of the axis's tags, so $var.AXIS is empty on the runs those options are picked. Add a tag from the axis to those options, or leave it if empty is intended.

sections.title: After a run (WP Debug → Warnings)
sections.text:
These only become clear during an actual generation:
What it flags | Severity | What it means
Unknown variable | warn | A $variable used in a template or combine was never set by any module, so it resolved to empty.
Unresolved reference | warn | An @{…} nested reference couldn't be resolved — its target wildcard wasn't found, or wasn't upstream.
Reference nested too deep | warn | Nested @{…} references went past the depth limit and stopped expanding.
Circular reference | warn | A loop of @{…} references pointed back at itself; it was broken to avoid hanging.
Variable used where it can't be | warn | A $variable was read somewhere that doesn't support one (for example, inside a wildcard option).
Sub-category filter matched nothing | warn | An @{…} sub-category filter matched no options, so the reference resolved to nothing (empty).
Fixed Values override unreadable | warn | A Fixed Values instance's per-instance overrides couldn't be read, so they were ignored.
Unknown constraint mode | warn | A constraint used a reweight mode that isn't recognised; that entry was skipped.
Factor ignored (Allow) | info | A factor was set together with mode Allow, where the factor has no effect.
Constraint source missing at run | warn | The constraint's source wildcard wasn't present in the stack when the run reached it.
Constraint excluded everything | warn | Reweighting zeroed out every option on the target, so it resolved to nothing. Give the target a fallback option to have it stand in instead (Debug then shows "Fallback used").
Constraint never fired | info | A constraint was set up but its target wildcard never came up this run, so it had no effect.
Invalid injector name | warn | A WP Context Injector row used a variable name that isn't valid.
Reserved injector name | warn | A WP Context Injector row tried to use a name starting with __, which is reserved internally.
